live_plab_copy.stem: Which contraceptive method provides long-term contraception and is placed inside the uterus?

options.A: Combined oral contraceptive pill

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Intrauterine device or system
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Intrauterine contraceptive methods are inserted into the uterine cavity and provide long-term contraception.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. The combined pill is taken orally. B. The condom is a barrier method. C. The implant is inserted under the skin. E. The patch is applied to the skin.
live_plab_copy.pearl: The copper IUD and hormonal IUS are long-acting reversible contraceptives placed in the uterus; LARC methods are more effective than user-dependent methods.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Long-term contraception ↓ Placed inside the uterus ↓ Copper device or levonorgestrel system ↓ Intrauterine device or system
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, contraceptive implant — also long-acting and reversible, which tempts, but it sits under the skin of the upper arm, not inside the uterus.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: The IUD and IUS are the intrauterine long-acting methods.

live_plab_copy.stem: A woman is found to have anti-D antibodies during pregnancy. Why is this clinically important?

options.A: It indicates a raised risk of fetal neural tube defect
options.C: It predicts maternal thrombocytopenia later in pregnancy
options.D: It risks haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. It risks haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Maternal red-cell antibodies can cross the placenta and cause fetal or neonatal haemolysis.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Anti-D antibodies do not indicate a risk of neural tube defects. B. Anti-D antibodies do not diagnose iron deficiency. C. Anti-D antibodies target fetal red cells and do not predict maternal thrombocytopenia. E. Gestational diabetes is diagnosed using glucose testing.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Once maternal anti-D antibodies are present, prophylactic anti-D no longer helps; the pregnancy needs specialist fetal medicine monitoring for fetal anaemia.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Maternal anti-D antibodies ↓ IgG crosses the placenta ↓ Destroys RhD-positive fetal red cells ↓ Haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, maternal thrombocytopenia — antibodies in pregnancy may suggest immune thrombocytopenia, but anti-D targets red cells and the fetus is at risk.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Maternal anti-D antibodies threaten the fetus with haemolysis.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 58-year-old woman has recurrent postmenopausal bleeding. Examination reveals a visible lesion arising from the cervix. What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Treat with an antifungal cream only
options.C: Reassurance because cervical lesions are always benign

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Urgent gynaecological assessment
live_plab_copy.why_correct: A visible cervical lesion with postmenopausal bleeding requires appropriate assessment for significant cervical pathology, including malignancy.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Antifungal treatment is inappropriate without evidence of candidiasis. B. HRT is not treatment for an unexplained cervical lesion. C. Cervical lesions are not invariably benign. D. Persistent postmenopausal bleeding should not simply be observed.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A visible cervical lesion with postmenopausal bleeding must be assessed urgently for cervical cancer; a cervical screening test is not the right tool for a symptomatic, visible lesion.
live_plab_copy.thinking: 58-year-old with recurrent postmenopausal bleeding ↓ Visible lesion on the cervix ↓ Possible cervical malignancy ↓ Urgent gynaecological assessment
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, reassurance because cervical lesions are always benign — polyps and ectropion are common, but no visible lesion with postmenopausal bleeding can be assumed benign without assessment.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: A visible cervical lesion with postmenopausal bleeding needs urgent gynaecological referral.

live_plab_copy.stem: During labour, a fetal hand is felt alongside the presenting part. What is this an example of?

options.A: Cord prolapse

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Compound presentation
live_plab_copy.why_correct: A limb presenting alongside another fetal presenting part is a compound presentation.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Cord prolapse involves the umbilical cord descending ahead of the presenting part. C. Occipitoposterior position describes the orientation of the fetal head, not a limb alongside the presenting part. D. Footling breech presentation means a foot presents first, rather than a hand alongside the head. E. Placenta praevia concerns placental location.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Compound presentation is a fetal limb, usually a hand, lying alongside the presenting part, most often the head; distinguish it from cord prolapse, an obstetric emergency.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Labour in progress ↓ Fetal hand felt on examination ↓ Lying alongside the presenting part ↓ Compound presentation
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, cord prolapse — also something felt beside the presenting part, but that is umbilical cord, not a limb; a hand alongside it is compound presentation.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: A limb beside the presenting part is compound presentation; cord beside it is cord prolapse.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman taking an oral contraceptive pill has significant vomiting shortly after taking a pill.

Why is this relevant?

options.A: She should take two pills daily for the rest of the current packet
options.B: Absorption may be reduced, so follow missed-pill advice for that pill
options.C: She should switch to a progestogen-only pill, which vomiting does not affect
options.D: Vomiting affects absorption only if it occurs more than 6 hours after a pill
options.E: She needs emergency contraception regardless of when she last had sex

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Absorption may be reduced, so follow missed-pill advice for that pill
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Vomiting soon after a pill (within 3 hours for combined pills; within 2 hours for traditional levonorgestrel or norethisterone POPs, or 3–4 hours for desogestrel or drospirenone POPs) may prevent absorption, so it is managed as a missed or late pill using FSRH guidance.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Doubling doses is not recommended and increases side effects. C. Vomiting soon after a progestogen-only pill can also prevent absorption. D. Absorption is affected by vomiting within about 2–4 hours of taking a pill, depending on pill type — not only after 6 hours. E. The need for emergency contraception depends on the pill type, timing and recent unprotected sex, as set out in missed-pill guidance.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Vomiting soon after taking a contraceptive pill may stop it being absorbed, so treat it as a missed or late pill and follow FSRH missed-pill advice for that pill type.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Taking an oral contraceptive ↓ Vomits shortly after a pill ↓ The hormone may not have been absorbed ↓ Treat it like a missed pill ↓ Absorption may be reduced, so follow missed-pill advice for that pill
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, switch to a progestogen-only pill — tempting as a simple fix. Vomiting soon after a progestogen-only pill also impairs absorption, so switching solves nothing.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Vomiting soon after a pill counts as a missed or late pill; apply missed-pill rules.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill asks whether it protects against sexually transmitted infections.

What is the correct advice?

options.A: It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections
options.B: It reduces viral STIs but not bacterial infections
options.C: It protects against HIV but not other infections
options.D: It gives protection against STIs similar to condoms
options.E: It protects against gonorrhoea but not chlamydia

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Combined hormonal contraception prevents pregnancy but does not provide STI protection.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. It does not protect against viral STIs. C. It does not provide protection against HIV. D. Condoms provide a degree of protection against many STIs; the combined pill does not. E. It does not specifically protect against gonorrhoea or chlamydia.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Hormonal contraception prevents pregnancy but gives no STI protection; advise condoms for STI protection, especially with new or multiple partners.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Combined pill user ↓ The pill works hormonally to prevent ovulation ↓ No barrier to pathogens ↓ No STI protection ↓ It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, protection similar to condoms — both are contraceptives so they seem equivalent, but only barrier methods reduce STI transmission.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: The pill prevents pregnancy, not STIs: use condoms as well.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman with six weeks of amenorrhoea develops severe abdominal pain and collapses. She has a positive pregnancy test and is hypotensive.

What is the priority?

options.A: Transvaginal ultrasound in the early pregnancy unit the next morning
options.B: Serial serum hCG measurements 48 hours apart
options.C: Analgesia and discharge with safety-netting advice and GP review
options.D: Intramuscular methotrexate for a presumed unruptured ectopic pregnancy
options.E: Emergency resuscitation for possible ruptured ectopic pregnancy

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Emergency resuscitation for possible ruptured ectopic pregnancy
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Abdominal pain and collapse with hypotension and a positive pregnancy test at six weeks indicate a ruptured ectopic pregnancy with haemorrhagic shock until proven otherwise. ABCDE resuscitation, cross-matched blood and immediate gynaecology referral for surgery are required (NICE NG126).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Delaying assessment would be dangerous in a shocked patient. B. Serial hCG monitoring is for stable patients and would delay life-saving treatment. C. Discharge in shock would be dangerous. D. Methotrexate is for stable unruptured ectopic pregnancy, not haemodynamic collapse.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Any woman of reproductive age who collapses with abdominal pain needs a pregnancy test; if positive and shocked, resuscitate and involve the gynaecology team for surgery immediately.
live_plab_copy.thinking: > Early pregnancy + pain + collapse  ↓  ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, methotrexate for a presumed unruptured ectopic — tempting because ectopic pregnancy is suspected, but methotrexate is only for stable patients; hypotension signals rupture needing surgery.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Positive pregnancy test, pain and shock: ruptured ectopic, so resuscitate and go to theatre.

live_plab_copy.stem: A woman taking a combined oral contraceptive pill misses pills and is unsure whether she remains protected.  What is the most important factor when assessing management?

options.A: Number and timing of missed active pills
options.B: Her current age and body mass index at review
options.C: Her blood pressure at her last pill review
options.D: How many years she has taken this pill brand

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Number and timing of missed active pills
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Management after missed combined pills depends on which pills were missed and when they were missed within the pill-taking cycle.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Age and BMI affect eligibility for combined hormonal contraception but not missed-pill management. C. Blood pressure does not determine missed-pill management. D. Duration of use does not determine missed-pill management. E. Eye colour is irrelevant.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Missed-pill risk in the COCP depends on where in the pack the pills were missed, since the pill-free interval is when the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis is most likely to recover and ovulation to resume.
live_plab_copy.thinking: This question tests whether you know that missed-pill guidance is not one-size-fits-all; the decisive variable is timing relative to the pill-free interval, not patient characteristics unrelated to the contraceptive mechanism.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: Weaker candidates sometimes look for a single 'magic number' of missed pills rather than recognising that timing within the cycle is the determining factor.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: With missed COCP pills, it's not just how many — it's exactly when in the cycle they were missed.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman at 36 weeks reports that her baby's movements have noticeably reduced.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Wait until the next routine antenatal appointment
options.B: Reassure her that reduced movement is always normal near term
options.D: Prompt assessment according to the maternity pathway
options.E: Ignore the change if there is no pain

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Prompt assessment according to the maternity pathway
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Reduced fetal movements may indicate fetal compromise, so the woman should contact maternity services and be assessed promptly with CTG monitoring.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Waiting delays assessment of possible fetal compromise. B. Fetal movements should continue until labour, so a reduction should not be dismissed. C. Exercise does not assess fetal wellbeing and is not an appropriate response. E. Reduced movements need assessment whether or not there is pain.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Reduced fetal movements may be the first sign of fetal compromise. The woman should contact maternity services straight away for assessment, including CTG; never wait for the next appointment.
live_plab_copy.thinking: 36 weeks' gestation ↓ Noticeably reduced fetal movements ↓ Movements should continue until labour ↓ Possible fetal compromise ↓ Prompt assessment according to the maternity pathway
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, reduced movement is always normal near term — a common myth. Fetal movements should continue until labour, so a reduction must be assessed promptly.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Reduced fetal movements: prompt same-day maternity assessment, never wait.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A pregnant woman is found to have hyperglycaemia during routine antenatal testing despite having no symptoms.

Which diagnosis should be considered?

options.A: Phaeochromocytoma

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Gestational diabetes
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Hyperglycaemia first recognised during pregnancy may represent gestational diabetes.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension and is rare. B. Addison disease tends to cause hypoglycaemia, not hyperglycaemia. D. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria with normal blood glucose. E. Hyperglycaemia first detected in pregnancy is most likely gestational diabetes, not necessarily type 1 diabetes.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Gestational diabetes is often asymptomatic and found on testing; it raises risks of macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycaemia and needs glucose testing after birth.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Hyperglycaemia on routine antenatal testing ↓ No symptoms ↓ First recognised in pregnancy ↓ C, gestational diabetes
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, type 1 diabetes only — tempting as a cause of hyperglycaemia, but asymptomatic hyperglycaemia found on antenatal testing most likely reflects gestational diabetes.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Hyperglycaemia first found in pregnancy is usually gestational diabetes.

live_plab_copy.stem: A woman has heavy vaginal bleeding shortly after giving birth. What is the most important immediate principle?

options.A: Encourage breastfeeding and reassess the bleeding in one hour
options.B: Treat as postpartum haemorrhage and escalate urgently
options.C: Give oral iron and recheck the haemoglobin level tomorrow
options.D: Observe as normal lochia and review at 6 weeks
options.E: Restrict IV fluids to avoid pulmonary oedema

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Treat as postpartum haemorrhage and escalate urgently
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Significant postpartum bleeding can rapidly become life-threatening and requires immediate assessment, resuscitation and identification of the cause.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Delay is unsafe with heavy bleeding. C. Oral iron does not treat acute haemorrhage. D. Heavy bleeding is not normal lochia. E. Fluid restriction would worsen hypovolaemia.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In postpartum haemorrhage, call for help and resuscitate while finding the cause with the four Ts: tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin; uterine atony is the commonest.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Recent birth ↓ Heavy vaginal bleeding ↓ Potentially life-threatening haemorrhage ↓ Resuscitate and find the cause ↓ Treat as postpartum haemorrhage and escalate urgently
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, observing as normal lochia — some bleeding after birth is normal, which tempts, but heavy bleeding is not lochia; delay risks rapid maternal collapse.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Heavy bleeding after birth is PPH: escalate and resuscitate immediately.

live_plab_copy.stem: What is the main purpose of HPV vaccination?

options.A: To prevent HPV-related cancers and genital warts
options.B: To prevent genital herpes and other sexual infections
options.D: To clear existing cervical HPV infection
options.E: To replace the need for cervical screening

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. To prevent HPV-related cancers and genital warts
live_plab_copy.why_correct: HPV vaccination protects against important HPV types responsible for cervical and several other HPV-related diseases.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Genital herpes is caused by herpes simplex virus, and HPV vaccine does not protect against other STIs. C. The vaccine is preventive and does not treat existing warts. D. Vaccination does not clear established HPV infection. E. Vaccinated people should still attend cervical screening.
live_plab_copy.pearl: HPV vaccination is preventive: it protects against high-risk types causing cervical, anal and other cancers and against wart-causing types; it does not treat established infection.
live_plab_copy.thinking: HPV causes cancers and genital warts ↓ Vaccine induces immunity before exposure ↓ Prevents rather than treats infection ↓ A, prevent HPV-related cancers and warts
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, replacing cervical screening — tempting because the vaccine prevents most cervical cancers, but it does not cover every high-risk type, so screening continues.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: HPV vaccine prevents disease; vaccinated people still need cervical screening.

Which test should be performed promptly?

options.A: Troponin only

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, serum amylase only — a standard test in abdominal pain, but it cannot establish pregnancy status, which must be checked promptly to consider ectopic pregnancy.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Abdominal pain or bleeding in a woman of reproductive age: pregnancy test first.

live_plab_copy.stem: A pregnant woman is found to carry group B Streptococcus on a swab in the current pregnancy. What is the most appropriate intrapartum management to reduce early-onset neonatal infection?

options.A: Elective caesarean section for all carriers
options.B: A course of oral antibiotics now, in the antenatal period

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Intravenous benzylpenicillin during labour

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 38-year-old woman has heavy regular periods and fatigue. Her blood tests show iron-deficiency anaemia.

Which finding most directly explains the anaemia?

options.A: Increased vitamin B12 requirement

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Chronic blood loss
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Persistent heavy menstrual bleeding can cause chronic iron loss leading to iron-deficiency anaemia.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia, not iron deficiency. B. Folate malabsorption causes macrocytic anaemia, not iron deficiency. C. Haemolysis does not usually cause iron deficiency and would typically cause a raised reticulocyte count and jaundice. E. Reduced erythropoietin (as in CKD) causes normocytic anaemia, not iron deficiency.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Heavy menstrual bleeding is a leading cause of iron-deficiency anaemia in premenopausal women, as repeated blood loss drains iron stores faster than diet replaces them.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Heavy regular periods ↓ Fatigue ↓ Iron-deficiency anaemia ↓ Iron lost through repeated bleeding ↓ Chronic blood loss
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, increased haemolysis — it causes anaemia, but haemolysis does not usually cause iron deficiency and typically gives jaundice and a raised reticulocyte count.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Iron deficiency points to blood loss; in a menstruating woman, think heavy periods.

Which diagnosis should be considered?

options.A: Genital herpes

Vulvovaginal candidiasis causes itch with thick white discharge and erythema rather than pale thin skin with architectural change. C. live_plab_copy.pearl: Lichen sclerosus gives itchy, white, thin 'cigarette-paper' vulval skin with loss of normal architecture; treat with a potent topical steroid and keep under review because of the small risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Postmenopausal woman with chronic vulval itch ↓ Skin is pale and thin, not red or ulcerated ↓ Architectural change (labial fusion or resorption) points to a chronic scarring dermatosis ↓ Lichen sclerosus
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, vulvovaginal candidiasis — itch makes it tempting, but thrush gives red, inflamed skin with thick white discharge and does not cause pale atrophic skin or architectural change.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Chronic vulval itch plus pale, thin skin and scarring means lichen sclerosus until proven otherwise.

live_plab_copy.stem: A pregnant woman who is rhesus D-negative gives birth to a rhesus D-positive baby. What is the purpose of anti-D immunoglobulin?

options.A: Treat haemolytic disease in this newborn baby
options.C: Reduce maternal haemolysis in the days after delivery
options.D: Prevent neonatal jaundice in this newborn baby

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Prevent maternal anti-D antibody formation
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Anti-D reduces the risk of maternal antibody formation against rhesus D-positive fetal red cells.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Anti-D is prophylaxis for future pregnancies, not treatment of the current baby. B. It has no role in preventing haemorrhage. C. It does not treat maternal haemolysis. D. Neonatal jaundice requires assessment and treatment according to bilirubin levels and cause.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Anti-D works by preventing sensitisation of an RhD-negative mother; once she has formed anti-D antibodies it cannot help, which is why timely doses after delivery and sensitising events matter.
live_plab_copy.thinking: RhD-negative mother ↓ RhD-positive baby; fetal cells enter her circulation ↓ Sensitisation would threaten future RhD-positive pregnancies ↓ Anti-D prevents maternal antibody formation
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, treat haemolytic disease in this newborn — tempting because HDFN is the concern, but anti-D is given to the mother to protect future pregnancies.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Anti-D is maternal prophylaxis that protects future pregnancies.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A pregnant woman has persistent vomiting with dehydration and inability to maintain oral intake.

What should be considered?

options.A: Normal pregnancy sickness to be managed with dietary advice at home
options.B: Hyperemesis gravidarum needing hydration and nutritional assessment
options.C: Gestational diabetes requiring a glucose tolerance test
options.D: Gastroenteritis to be treated with oral rehydration at home
options.E: Diabetes insipidus requiring a water deprivation test

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Hyperemesis gravidarum needing hydration and nutritional assessment
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Persistent vomiting with dehydration and inability to keep food or fluids down suggests hyperemesis gravidarum, which needs assessment of hydration, electrolytes and ketones, and antiemetics with fluids where required (RCOG guidance).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Dehydration and inability to maintain oral intake go beyond normal nausea and vomiting of pregnancy. C. Gestational diabetes does not cause persistent vomiting with dehydration. D. Persistent vomiting with dehydration in pregnancy suggests hyperemesis gravidarum, and home oral rehydration is inadequate when intake cannot be maintained. E. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and thirst, not persistent vomiting.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Hyperemesis gravidarum differs from normal pregnancy sickness by dehydration or inability to keep food and fluids down; it needs assessment, antiemetics and fluids where required.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Persistent vomiting with dehydration ↓ Unable to maintain oral intake ↓ Hyperemesis gravidarum needing hydration and nutritional assessment
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, normal pregnancy sickness — nausea and vomiting are common in pregnancy, but dehydration and inability to maintain intake go beyond it and need assessment.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Vomiting in pregnancy with dehydration: hyperemesis gravidarum, not ordinary pregnancy sickness.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Irregular tightenings without cervical change = Braxton Hicks, not labour.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Jaundice on the combined pill is never normal: stop it and investigate.

live_plab_copy.pearl: Menopause is diagnosed clinically in women over 45 after 12 months without periods; FSH testing is not usually needed in this age group.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Woman aged 52 ↓ Irregular periods, then none ↓ 12 months of amenorrhoea ↓ No other concerning features ↓ Menopause
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, Cervical cancer — cancer worries tempt, but it causes abnormal bleeding, not amenorrhoea; bleeding after the menopause would need investigation.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Over 45 with 12 months of amenorrhoea, menopause is a clinical diagnosis.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its impact on the woman's life.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman requests emergency contraception after unprotected sexual intercourse.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Offer levonorgestrel only, as the copper IUD is reserved for failed pills
options.B: Wait for a pregnancy test in three weeks' time before offering any treatment
options.C: Assess timing and circumstances and promptly discuss suitable options
options.D: Give ulipristal and advise starting the combined pill the next day
options.E: Advise that emergency contraception is ineffective after 24 hours

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Assess timing and circumstances and promptly discuss suitable options
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Emergency contraception is time-sensitive, so the timing of unprotected sex, cycle details and other risks should be assessed promptly, with the copper IUD (most effective), ulipristal acetate and levonorgestrel discussed (FSRH guidance).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception and should be offered first-line to eligible women. B. Delay reduces effectiveness, and waiting for a pregnancy test is inappropriate. D. After ulipristal, hormonal contraception should be delayed for 5 days because it can reduce ulipristal's effect. E. Oral methods are licensed up to 72 or 120 hours and the copper IUD up to 5 days, so emergency contraception remains effective after 24 hours.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Emergency contraception is time-critical: establish the timing of intercourse and the cycle, and offer the copper IUD as the most effective option alongside ulipristal acetate or levonorgestrel.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Request for emergency contraception ↓ Effectiveness depends on timing and method ↓ Assess timing, cycle and risks promptly ↓ Discuss copper IUD, ulipristal and levonorgestrel without delay
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, ineffective after 24 hours — earlier use is better, but oral methods and the copper IUD remain options well beyond 24 hours, so no one should be turned away on that basis.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Emergency contraception: assess timing promptly and discuss all options; the copper IUD is most effective.

A woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is planning a pregnancy.

What is the most appropriate principle?

options.A: Pregnancy is absolutely contraindicated
options.B: Standard midwife-led antenatal care without extra monitoring
options.C: Stop hydroxychloroquine before conception to avoid fetal harm
options.D: Pre-pregnancy specialist assessment and medication review

live_plab_copy.thinking: SLE planning pregnancy ↓ Risks of flare and pregnancy complications ↓ Some drugs teratogenic, others continued ↓ D, pre-pregnancy specialist review
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, stop hydroxychloroquine — tempting as many drugs are stopped before conception, but hydroxychloroquine is usually continued because stopping it risks a lupus flare.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: SLE and pregnancy: plan ahead, review medicines, keep hydroxychloroquine, specialist care.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: After unprotected sex: offer emergency contraception promptly; the copper IUD is most effective.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman of reproductive age presents with lower abdominal pain.

Why is pregnancy testing important?

options.A: A positive test confirms that the pain is due to the pregnancy
options.B: Pregnancy status can alter the differential diagnosis and management
options.C: It is needed only before surgery or imaging using ionising radiation
options.D: A negative test excludes ectopic pregnancy and ovarian torsion
options.E: It is needed only if the patient reports a missed period

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Pregnancy status can alter the differential diagnosis and management
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Pregnancy status changes the differential diagnosis (for example, ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage) and influences imaging, prescribing and management decisions.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Pregnancy does not exclude other causes of abdominal pain such as appendicitis. C. Pregnancy status is relevant to assessment, diagnosis and prescribing, not only surgery or imaging. D. A negative test does not exclude ovarian torsion or other gynaecological conditions. E. Pregnancy can occur without a reported missed period, so testing should not depend on it.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain, a pregnancy test is essential: a positive result raises ectopic pregnancy and changes imaging, prescribing and surgical decisions.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Woman of reproductive age with lower abdominal pain ↓ Pregnancy may be unrecognised ↓ A positive status adds ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage and alters investigations and drugs ↓ Pregnancy status changes the differential and management
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, testing only after a missed period — it sounds logical, but pregnancy can occur without a reported missed period, so testing must not depend on the menstrual history.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Abdominal pain in a woman of reproductive age: test for pregnancy, whatever the menstrual history.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A pregnant woman has no urinary symptoms, but urine testing identifies significant bacteriuria.

Why is this clinically important?

options.A: It indicates pre-eclampsia is developing
options.B: It needs no treatment unless urinary symptoms develop
options.C: It suggests that gestational diabetes has developed
options.D: It is a likely contaminant that can be disregarded
options.E: It should be treated to prevent pyelonephritis

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. It should be treated to prevent pyelonephritis
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy reduces the risk of progression to symptomatic urinary infection and pyelonephritis.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Pre-eclampsia is characterised by hypertension and organ involvement, not bacteriuria. B. Pregnancy is an exception to the usual approach of not treating asymptomatic bacteriuria. C. Bacteriuria does not diagnose diabetes. D. Significant bacteriuria in pregnancy should be treated, not disregarded.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is screened for at booking and treated in pregnancy, unlike in most non-pregnant adults, because untreated it can progress to pyelonephritis.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant, no urinary symptoms ↓ Significant bacteriuria on testing ↓ Pregnancy favours ascending infection ↓ Treat to prevent pyelonephritis
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, no treatment unless symptoms develop — correct for most non-pregnant adults, which is why it tempts, but pregnancy is a key exception.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A pregnant woman at 10 weeks' gestation has persistent vomiting, poor oral intake and clinical dehydration.

Which is the most appropriate initial management principle?

options.A: Oral metoclopramide and review in one week
options.B: Reassurance and advice on small, frequent meals
options.C: Assess and correct dehydration and electrolytes
options.D: Nil by mouth to rest the gut for 24 hours
options.E: Start oral prednisolone as first-line therapy

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Assess and correct dehydration and electrolytes

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. A clinically dehydrated woman with poor oral intake needs assessment and fluid correction, not outpatient review in a week. B. Dietary advice alone is inappropriate in a dehydrated patient with persistent vomiting. D. Withholding oral intake without replacing fluids would worsen dehydration. E. Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory hyperemesis and are not first-line.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Severe vomiting in pregnancy is a clinical problem requiring assessment of hydration, nutrition and complications.
live_plab_copy.thinking: 10 weeks pregnant ↓ Persistent vomiting with poor intake ↓ Clinically dehydrated ↓ Fluid and electrolyte deficit is the immediate risk ↓ Assess and correct dehydration and electrolytes
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, reassurance and small frequent meals — fine for mild nausea of pregnancy, but a clinically dehydrated woman who cannot keep intake down needs assessment and rehydration.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Pregnancy vomiting with dehydration: assess and correct fluids and electrolytes first.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Contractions plus cervical change before 37 weeks equals preterm labour.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Amenorrhoea with menopausal symptoms under 40: think premature ovarian insufficiency.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, mild headache — headache warnings on the pill matter, but a mild self-resolving headache is not the red flag; a new severe headache or focal symptoms would be.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: On the combined pill, sudden chest pain and breathlessness means possible PE until proven otherwise.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Urinary symptoms in pregnancy: culture the urine and treat UTI promptly.

options.A: Treat maternal anaemia

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Prevent maternal rhesus sensitisation
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Anti-D binds fetal rhesus-positive red cells that enter the maternal circulation, reducing the risk of maternal antibody formation.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. It does not treat iron-deficiency or other maternal anaemia. B. It does not prevent pre-eclampsia. C. It does not treat gestational diabetes. E. It does not directly increase fetal haemoglobin.
live_plab_copy.pearl: After a potentially sensitising event in an RhD-negative woman, anti-D is given as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours; a Kleihauer test estimates the size of any fetomaternal haemorrhage.
live_plab_copy.thinking: RhD-negative pregnant woman ↓ Sensitising event lets fetal cells enter her blood ↓ Anti-D clears them before antibodies form ↓ Prevent maternal rhesus sensitisation
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, increase fetal haemoglobin directly — it links anti-D to the fetus, but anti-D acts on the mother's immune response and does not raise fetal haemoglobin.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Anti-D prevents maternal sensitisation; it is prophylaxis, not treatment.

live_plab_copy.stem:
During a vaginal delivery, the baby's head delivers but then retracts against the mother's perineum and the shoulders do not deliver with normal traction.

What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Apply fundal pressure
options.B: Perform an episiotomy as the only intervention
options.D: Pull firmly on the baby's head

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Perform the McRoberts manoeuvre
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency. The McRoberts manoeuvre is the initial manoeuvre used to help release the impacted anterior shoulder.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Fundal pressure can worsen impaction and should be avoided. B. Episiotomy may facilitate internal manoeuvres but does not itself release the impacted shoulder. D. Excessive traction on the head risks brachial plexus injury. E. Delay increases the risk of fetal hypoxia.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Shoulder dystocia: call for help, then McRoberts (hyperflexing the hips) with suprapubic pressure; never use fundal pressure or excessive traction on the head.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Head delivers then retracts (turtle sign) ↓ Shoulders do not deliver with normal traction ↓ Shoulder dystocia ↓ First manoeuvre to free the anterior shoulder ↓ McRoberts manoeuvre
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, pulling firmly on the head — instinctive when delivery stalls, but excessive traction does not free the impacted shoulder and risks brachial plexus injury.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Turtle sign means shoulder dystocia: call for help and start with McRoberts, never fundal pressure.

A pregnant woman has persistent vomiting, cannot keep fluids down and is becoming dehydrated.

What complication should be assessed for?

options.A: Gestational diabetes causing an osmotic diuresis and fluid depletion
options.B: Diabetes insipidus causing polyuria and excessive thirst
options.C: Iron-deficiency anaemia as the underlying cause of the nausea and vomiting
options.D: Acute appendicitis as the underlying cause of the persistent vomiting
options.E: Dehydration and electrolyte disturbance from hyperemesis gravidarum

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Dehydration and electrolyte disturbance from hyperemesis gravidarum
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Persistent vomiting with inability to keep fluids down suggests hyperemesis gravidarum, so the woman should be assessed for dehydration, ketosis and electrolyte disturbance such as hypokalaemia.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Gestational diabetes does not cause persistent vomiting and is not a complication of it. B. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and thirst, not persistent vomiting. C. Iron deficiency does not cause persistent vomiting with dehydration. D. Appendicitis can occur in pregnancy but is not the expected complication of persistent vomiting.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In hyperemesis gravidarum, assess for dehydration, ketosis and electrolyte disturbance, especially hypokalaemia. Thiamine is given when vomiting is prolonged, to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant ↓ Persistent vomiting ↓ Cannot keep fluids down ↓ Becoming dehydrated ↓ Dehydration and electrolyte disturbance from hyperemesis gravidarum
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, acute appendicitis — tempting because appendicitis can occur in pregnancy. Nothing in the stem suggests it, and persistent vomiting with dehydration fits hyperemesis.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Hyperemesis: assess hydration, ketones and electrolytes, and replace fluids.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman who is not immune to rubella becomes infected early in pregnancy.

Why is this clinically important?

options.A: It can cause congenital abnormalities in the fetus
options.B: It mainly causes severe maternal pneumonia
options.C: It mainly risks preterm labour without fetal defects
options.D: It increases the risk of gestational diabetes
options.E: It mainly harms the fetus in the third trimester

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. It can cause congenital abnormalities in the fetus
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Rubella infection during pregnancy can cause congenital rubella syndrome, including hearing, eye and cardiac abnormalities.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Rubella is usually mild in the mother; severe pneumonia is not its main risk. C. The main concern is congenital rubella syndrome, not preterm labour. D. Rubella is not a cause of gestational diabetes. E. Fetal risk is greatest with infection in early pregnancy.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Rubella in early pregnancy can cause congenital rubella syndrome: sensorineural deafness, cataracts and congenital heart disease. Fetal risk is greatest early in pregnancy.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Non-immune woman ↓ Rubella infection early in pregnancy ↓ Virus crosses the placenta during organogenesis ↓ A, congenital abnormalities in the fetus
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, mainly third-trimester harm — tempting because some infections matter more late in pregnancy, but rubella's fetal risk is highest in early pregnancy.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Rubella early in pregnancy threatens the fetus: deafness, eye and heart defects.

A 29-year-old woman starts a combined oral contraceptive pill. She asks when contraceptive protection begins.

options.E: Cycle day on which the pill was started

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, body mass index — it is relevant to COC prescribing, but it affects eligibility and risk, not when contraceptive protection begins.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: The start day of the cycle decides whether extra contraception is needed with a new combined pill.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, reassure her that this is normal — tempting if bleeding is light or atrophy seems likely, but postmenopausal bleeding is never normal and needs urgent investigation.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Any postmenopausal bleeding needs urgent assessment for endometrial cancer.

A woman taking a combined oral contraceptive pill develops significant vomiting.

Why might this matter?

options.A: It may reduce absorption and contraceptive effectiveness
options.B: It significantly increases the risk of venous thrombosis
options.C: It increases circulating oestrogen and side effects
options.D: It is a sign of early pregnancy despite the pill

live_plab_copy.why_correct: Vomiting within 3 hours of taking a combined pill may prevent absorption, so another pill should be taken as soon as possible; if vomiting persists, FSRH missed-pill guidance should be followed.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Vomiting does not significantly increase thrombosis risk. C. Vomiting reduces rather than increases hormone absorption. D. Vomiting in a pill user should not be assumed to indicate pregnancy. E. Vomiting does not interact with the pill to cause liver toxicity.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Vomiting soon after taking a combined pill may prevent absorption. Take another pill promptly; if vomiting persists, follow the missed-pill rules.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Combined pill user ↓ significant vomiting ↓ the tablet may be lost before absorption ↓ reduced contraceptive effectiveness
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, venous thrombosis risk — VTE is the best-known combined-pill risk, so it springs to mind, but vomiting does not significantly raise it; the concern is lost absorption.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Vomiting on the combined pill threatens absorption: treat it like a possible missed pill.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman with a positive pregnancy test has a transvaginal ultrasound showing neither a definite intrauterine nor an ectopic pregnancy. She is clinically stable.

Which principle is most appropriate?

options.A: Serum hCG alone can determine the location of the pregnancy
options.B: She can be discharged if the hCG is below 1,500 IU/L
options.C: A single low hCG result excludes ectopic pregnancy
options.D: Arrange follow-up: ectopic pregnancy is possible until located
options.E: An empty uterus on scan confirms a complete miscarriage has occurred

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Arrange follow-up: ectopic pregnancy is possible until located
live_plab_copy.why_correct: NICE states that a pregnancy of unknown location could be ectopic until the location is determined. Serial assessment and appropriate follow-up are required. Source: NICE NG126, Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Serum hCG should not be used alone to determine pregnancy location. B. A low hCG does not exclude ectopic pregnancy; follow-up and safety-netting are required. C. A single hCG result cannot exclude ectopic pregnancy. E. Absence of a visible pregnancy does not establish complete miscarriage.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In early pregnancy, symptoms can outweigh a reassuring-looking previous result; worsening pain or bleeding requires reassessment.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Positive pregnancy + no confirmed location  ↓  pregnancy of unknown location  ↓  follow-up + safety-netting.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, discharge if hCG is below 1,500 — a low hCG feels reassuring, but an ectopic pregnancy can occur at low hCG levels, so follow-up is still needed.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: A pregnancy of unknown location may be ectopic until located: arrange follow-up and safety-net.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A pregnant woman who is not known to be immune has been exposed to chickenpox.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Give the live varicella vaccine within 3 days of exposure
options.B: Reassure her and advise review if a rash later appears
options.C: Prescribe a 7-day course of oral antibiotics as prophylaxis
options.D: Arrange prompt assessment and check her VZV immunity
options.E: Arrange a detailed fetal anomaly scan the following week

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Arrange prompt assessment and check her VZV immunity
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Varicella infection during pregnancy can cause maternal and fetal complications, so an exposed non-immune pregnant woman requires appropriate assessment.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Live vaccines such as varicella vaccine are contraindicated during pregnancy. B. Chickenpox can cause significant maternal and fetal complications, so prompt assessment is needed before any rash. C. Antibiotics do not treat or prevent varicella. E. A scan does not address urgent assessment of immunity and post-exposure management.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A pregnant woman exposed to chickenpox needs prompt assessment: confirm the exposure, check her history and, if uncertain, her VZV antibodies, so post-exposure prophylaxis can be given if she is not immune.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant, not known to be immune ↓ Chickenpox exposure ↓ Risk of severe maternal and fetal disease ↓ D, prompt assessment and VZV immunity check
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, live varicella vaccine — post-exposure vaccination is used outside pregnancy, but live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Chickenpox exposure in pregnancy: check immunity promptly; never give a live vaccine.

live_plab_copy.stem: A pregnant woman develops dysuria and urinary frequency. Why is a urinary tract infection particularly important to recognise during pregnancy?

options.A: It is a recognised cause of neural tube defects
options.B: It does not need treatment if symptoms are mild
options.D: It is usually caused by sexually transmitted organisms
options.E: It indicates gestational diabetes until proven otherwise

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. It can progress to pyelonephritis
live_plab_copy.why_correct: UTIs during pregnancy warrant appropriate assessment and treatment because infection can progress and is associated with maternal and pregnancy complications.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. UTI is not a cause of neural tube defects. B. Symptomatic UTI in pregnancy requires treatment. D. UTI is usually caused by enteric organisms such as E. coli. E. UTI does not indicate gestational diabetes.
live_plab_copy.pearl: UTI in pregnancy, including asymptomatic bacteriuria, should be treated because it can progress to pyelonephritis and is linked with preterm birth; send urine for culture.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Dysuria and frequency ↓ Urinary tract dilatation and stasis in pregnancy ↓ Infection ascends more easily ↓ It can progress to pyelonephritis
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, no treatment if mild — watchful waiting tempts for mild symptoms outside pregnancy, but symptomatic UTI in pregnancy must always be treated.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Always treat UTI in pregnancy because of the risk of pyelonephritis.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: LNG-IUS gives reliable contraception and lighter periods; the copper IUD may make them heavier.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 30-year-old pregnant woman is found to have iron-deficiency anaemia at routine antenatal testing.

Which dietary advice is appropriate?

options.A: Avoid all protein
options.C: Stop eating foods containing vitamin C

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Increase intake of iron-rich foods
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Iron-rich foods contribute to maintaining iron stores and are appropriate dietary advice in iron deficiency.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Protein restriction is not appropriate. C. Vitamin C can enhance iron absorption. D. Fruit juice alone cannot correct iron deficiency. E. Vegetables should not generally be avoided.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Antenatal iron deficiency is treated with oral iron, with dietary advice alongside: iron-rich foods such as red meat, pulses and fortified cereals, ideally with vitamin C and away from tea or coffee.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Iron-deficiency anaemia on routine testing ↓ Iron stores need replenishing ↓ Increase intake of iron-rich foods
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, stop eating foods containing vitamin C — reflects a muddled link between vitamin C and iron, but vitamin C actually enhances non-haem iron absorption.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: In iron deficiency, advise iron-rich foods; vitamin C helps absorption while tea and coffee hinder it.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation has BP 158/105, 2+ proteinuria, and headache. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Antihypertensives, magnesium sulphate and planned delivery
options.B: Bed rest, IV fluids and repeat BP in 4 hours on the antenatal ward
options.C: Oral labetalol and twice-weekly day-unit review as an outpatient
options.D: Immediate caesarean section before controlling the BP or giving magnesium

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Antihypertensives, magnesium sulphate and planned delivery
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Severe pre-eclampsia: admit, antihypertensives (labetalol IV or oral nifedipine), magnesium sulphate for seizure prophylaxis (eclampsia prevention), and plan for delivery (a senior obstetric decision: at 34-36+6 weeks birth is planned when there are severe features such as ongoing severe headache or visual disturbance, uncontrolled BP or worsening bloods).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Bed rest and fluids do not control BP and risk fluid overload. C. Severe hypertension with proteinuria and headache requires admission, not outpatient care. D. BP must be controlled and magnesium sulphate given before delivery. E. Diuretics worsen intravascular depletion in pre-eclampsia.
live_plab_copy.pearl: MgSO4 reduces eclampsia risk by 50% in severe pre-eclampsia. Diazepam is not recommended for eclamptic seizures.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Severe pre-eclampsia = BP control + MgSO4 + delivery planning.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: Giving diuretics — pre-eclampsia causes vasoconstriction and relative hypovolaemia; diuretics worsen organ perfusion.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Severe pre-eclampsia: antihypertensives + MgSO4 seizure prophylaxis + plan for delivery.

options.D: Placenta praevia as a current pregnancy diagnosis

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Heavy bleeding after delivery is PPH: resuscitate and work through the 4 Ts.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A pregnant patient has persistent vomiting, cannot keep fluids down and has clinical signs of dehydration.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Advise ginger and small frequent meals with GP review next week
options.B: Reassure her that vomiting is normal and expected in pregnancy
options.C: Assess severity and treat as possible hyperemesis gravidarum
options.D: Prescribe oral ondansetron and review her again in two weeks' time
options.E: Advise fasting for 24 hours to settle the stomach before eating

Dehydration is a sign of significant disease that needs assessment and treatment, not reassurance. D. live_plab_copy.pearl: Vomiting in pregnancy with inability to keep fluids down and dehydration suggests hyperemesis gravidarum; assess severity, for example with a PUQE score, ketones and U&Es, and treat with antiemetics and IV fluids as needed.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant ↓ Persistent vomiting ↓ Cannot keep fluids down ↓ Clinical dehydration ↓ Assess severity and treat as possible hyperemesis gravidarum
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, ginger and small frequent meals — these suit mild nausea and vomiting, but she cannot keep fluids down and is dehydrated, so needs assessment and rehydration now.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Vomiting in pregnancy with dehydration: assess for hyperemesis and rehydrate.

live_plab_copy.stem: A woman with an intact uterus is considering systemic hormone replacement therapy.  Why is a progestogen generally included when systemic oestrogen is prescribed?

options.A: To reduce the long-term risk of developing breast cancer
options.B: To reduce oestrogen-related venous thromboembolism risk
options.D: To prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer
options.E: To enhance relief of hot flushes and night sweats

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. To prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Unopposed systemic oestrogen stimulates the endometrium. Adding a progestogen provides endometrial protection in women with a uterus.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Adding a progestogen slightly increases, rather than reduces, breast cancer risk. B. A progestogen does not reduce VTE risk; oral HRT increases it. C. It does not directly increase thyroid hormone production. E. Oestrogen relieves vasomotor symptoms; the progestogen is added for endometrial protection.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Unopposed oestrogen drives continuous endometrial proliferation, so a progestogen is added in women with a uterus specifically to induce shedding or atrophy and prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer.
live_plab_copy.thinking: The clue 'intact uterus' is the key discriminator: in a woman without a uterus, oestrogen-only HRT is used, so the question is really testing why the uterus changes the prescribing decision.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: Candidates sometimes assume the progestogen is for symptom control (hot flushes) rather than for its specific endometrial-protective role.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Uterus present on HRT: add a progestogen to protect the endometrium, not for symptom control.

live_plab_copy.stem: A pregnant woman has a routine antenatal blood test showing antibodies that could affect the fetus. What is the main concern?

options.A: Gestational diabetes mellitus

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Fetal and neonatal haemolytic disease

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Red-cell antibodies do not cause gestational diabetes. B. Obstetric cholestasis is diagnosed by itch and raised bile acids, not antibody screening. D. Antibody positivity does not by itself diagnose placental abruption. E. Pre-eclampsia is defined by hypertension with proteinuria or organ dysfunction.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Maternal red-cell antibodies such as anti-D can cross the placenta and haemolyse fetal red cells, so their detection needs monitoring for fetal anaemia and neonatal jaundice.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, pre-eclampsia — it is a major antenatal concern, but it is diagnosed by hypertension with proteinuria or organ dysfunction, not by red-cell antibodies.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Red-cell antibodies in pregnancy mean risk of haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman with prolonged unopposed oestrogen exposure develops abnormal uterine bleeding.

Which condition can precede endometrial cancer?

options.A: Endometrial hyperplasia

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Endometrial hyperplasia
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Endometrial hyperplasia, particularly atypical hyperplasia, can be associated with progression to endometrial cancer.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Cervical ectropion is a benign cervical change and does not precede endometrial cancer. C. Vulvovaginal candidiasis is not premalignant. D. Bartholin cyst is a benign vulval cyst unrelated to endometrial cancer. E. Ovarian torsion is not a premalignant endometrial condition.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Unopposed oestrogen, for example from obesity, anovulation or oestrogen-only HRT with a uterus, drives endometrial hyperplasia; atypical hyperplasia carries a significant risk of progression to cancer.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Prolonged unopposed oestrogen ↓ Endometrial proliferation ↓ Abnormal uterine bleeding ↓ Hyperplasia, especially atypical ↓ A, endometrial hyperplasia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, cervical ectropion — tempting as a cause of abnormal bleeding, but it is a benign cervical change and does not precede endometrial cancer.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Unopposed oestrogen causes endometrial hyperplasia, a precursor of endometrial cancer.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding two years after her last menstrual period. What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Reassure her that this is normal
options.C: Prescribe contraception and review in one year

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, reassure her that this is normal — irregular bleeding is common around the menopause, but bleeding after a year without periods is never normal.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Postmenopausal bleeding always needs investigation.

live_plab_copy.stem: A pregnant woman is found to be rhesus D negative. Why may anti-D immunoglobulin be required?

options.A: To treat hyperemesis gravidarum in the first trimester
options.B: To prevent haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
options.C: To reduce the risk of group B streptococcal infection
options.D: To lower the risk of pre-eclampsia in later pregnancy

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. To prevent haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Anti-D immunoglobulin reduces maternal sensitisation to rhesus D antigen and therefore reduces the risk of haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Anti-D does not treat vomiting in pregnancy. C. Anti-D does not prevent group B streptococcal infection. D. Anti-D does not reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia. E. Anti-D does not treat iron-deficiency anaemia.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Anti-D prevents an RhD-negative mother forming anti-D antibodies that could cross the placenta in a later pregnancy and destroy RhD-positive fetal red cells.
live_plab_copy.thinking: RhD-negative mother ↓ RhD-positive fetal cells may enter her circulation ↓ Sensitisation produces maternal antibodies ↓ Anti-D prevents haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, correct iron-deficiency anaemia — anaemia is a common antenatal blood problem, but anti-D does not affect iron or haemoglobin; it only prevents RhD sensitisation.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Anti-D protects future babies from haemolytic disease.

live_plab_copy.stem: A woman has severe early-pregnancy vomiting, uterine size greater than expected for gestation and markedly elevated β-hCG. Ultrasound shows abnormal intrauterine tissue without a normal fetus. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Ectopic pregnancy

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Complete molar pregnancy
live_plab_copy.why_correct: A complete molar pregnancy is associated with very high β-hCG, excessive uterine size and abnormal intrauterine trophoblastic tissue without a normal fetus.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Ectopic pregnancy is extrauterine. B. Hyperemesis may occur with a molar pregnancy but does not explain the ultrasound findings. C. Placenta praevia is a later pregnancy placental location problem. D. A missed miscarriage involves a non-viable intrauterine pregnancy rather than molar tissue.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A complete hydatidiform mole classically presents with exaggerated pregnancy symptoms, uterus large-for-dates, markedly raised β-hCG, and no normal fetus on ultrasound.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Build the diagnosis from the ultrasound finding of abnormal trophoblastic tissue without a fetus, which rules out ectopic, missed miscarriage and praevia in one step.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: Hyperemesis gravidarum alone is an attractive distractor because the vomiting is so prominent, but it fails to explain the grossly elevated hCG and abnormal scan appearance.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: No fetus plus sky-high hCG equals molar pregnancy until proven otherwise.

A 57-year-old woman who has been postmenopausal for 6 years develops vaginal bleeding.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, vaginal oestrogen for atrophy — atrophy is a common cause, but it can only be accepted once endometrial cancer has been excluded.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Any postmenopausal bleeding: urgent referral to exclude endometrial cancer.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 32-year-old woman is found to have blood group RhD negative during pregnancy.

Which test is used to identify clinically significant red-cell antibodies in pregnancy?

options.A: Serum high-sensitivity troponin

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Antibody screening
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Antenatal antibody screening identifies maternal red-cell antibodies that may cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Troponin assesses myocardial injury. B. The Kleihauer test quantifies fetomaternal haemorrhage rather than detecting maternal red-cell antibodies. D. D-dimer is associated with thromboembolic assessment. E. HbA1c assesses longer-term glycaemic control.
live_plab_copy.pearl: All pregnant women have blood group and red-cell antibody screening at booking and again around 28 weeks; RhD-negative women without anti-D antibodies are offered routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis.
live_plab_copy.thinking: RhD-negative pregnant woman ↓ Risk of maternal red-cell antibodies ↓ Antibodies can cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn ↓ Antibody screening
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, Kleihauer–Betke test — closely linked with RhD-negative pregnancy, but it measures the volume of fetomaternal haemorrhage to guide anti-D dosing; it does not detect maternal antibodies.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Antibody screening detects red-cell antibodies; Kleihauer measures fetal cells in maternal blood.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Buttocks or feet presenting first = breech; offer ECV near term if suitable.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman who is 10 weeks pregnant asks whether she should continue taking folic acid.

What is the usual advice regarding folic acid supplementation?

options.A: Stop now, as the neural tube has already fully closed
options.B: Continue throughout pregnancy at a dose of 5 mg daily
options.C: Continue through the first 12 weeks of pregnancy
options.D: Avoid it now, as it may mask vitamin B12 deficiency

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Continue through the first 12 weeks of pregnancy
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Folic acid supplementation around conception and during the first trimester reduces the risk of neural tube defects.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Although the neural tube closes early, folic acid is advised until 12 weeks of pregnancy. B. The 5 mg dose is reserved for women at higher risk, and standard advice is 400 micrograms daily until 12 weeks. D. Folic acid is routinely recommended in early pregnancy, and concern about masking B12 deficiency is not a reason to avoid it. E. Stopping immediately after conception misses the key period of neural tube development.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Standard advice is folic acid 400 micrograms daily from before conception until 12 weeks; a 5 mg dose is reserved for higher-risk women, such as those with a previous neural tube defect, diabetes or antiepileptic use.
live_plab_copy.thinking: 10 weeks pregnant ↓ Still in the first trimester ↓ Folic acid reduces neural tube defect risk ↓ Continue until 12 weeks
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, continue throughout pregnancy at 5 mg daily — the high dose is real but only for higher-risk women, and routine supplementation stops at 12 weeks.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Folic acid: 400 micrograms daily from preconception to 12 weeks; 5 mg only if higher risk.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 36-year-old woman has severe unilateral pelvic pain occurring shortly after intercourse. She is haemodynamically stable and pregnancy testing is negative. Which diagnosis is most likely if ultrasound shows free fluid and a collapsed ovarian cyst?

options.A: Endometrial cancer

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Ruptured ovarian cyst
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Sudden pelvic pain with a collapsed ovarian cyst and free pelvic fluid is typical of a ruptured ovarian cyst.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Endometrial cancer typically presents with abnormal uterine bleeding. B. Pyelonephritis usually causes fever, flank pain and urinary symptoms. C. Ectopic pregnancy is very unlikely with a negative pregnancy test. D. Appendicitis usually causes right lower abdominal pain with gastrointestinal symptoms and would not explain the collapsed ovarian cyst.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A ruptured ovarian cyst often presents with sudden unilateral pain after intercourse or exercise; with a negative pregnancy test and stable observations, management is often conservative.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, ectopic pregnancy — pelvic pain with free fluid is the classic ectopic picture, but a negative pregnancy test and a collapsed ovarian cyst point elsewhere.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Pelvic pain with free fluid: check the pregnancy test, then read the ultrasound.

Which hormone does the commonly used UK implant release?

options.A: Oestrogen only

live_plab_copy.takeaway: The UK contraceptive implant is progestogen-only and releases etonogestrel.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 59-year-old woman presents with postmenopausal vaginal bleeding. She has had no bleeding for 8 years.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Ignore the bleeding unless it becomes painful
options.B: Treat empirically with antibiotics without assessment
options.D: Urgent assessment for possible endometrial pathology
options.E: Reassurance that this is normal after menopause

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Urgent assessment for possible endometrial pathology
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Postmenopausal bleeding is an important symptom requiring assessment because endometrial cancer is an important possible cause.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Pain is not required for significant endometrial pathology. B. Antibiotics do not address the important differential diagnosis. C. Cervical screening does not replace assessment of postmenopausal bleeding. E. Vaginal bleeding after menopause is not considered normal.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Postmenopausal bleeding needs urgent assessment for endometrial cancer, usually starting with transvaginal ultrasound to measure endometrial thickness.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Woman aged 59 ↓ No periods for 8 years ↓ New vaginal bleeding ↓ Endometrial cancer must be excluded ↓ Urgent assessment for possible endometrial pathology
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, routine cervical smear only — the cervix can bleed, but cervical screening does not assess the endometrium; this needs urgent assessment.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Any postmenopausal bleeding needs urgent assessment for endometrial cancer.

Influenza does not cause cervical cancer. E. HSV-2 was historically investigated as a cause but is not the principal cause of cervical cancer.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, HSV-2 — a sexually transmitted genital virus once suspected as the cause, but HPV, not herpes, drives cervical neoplasia.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Cervical cancer is driven by persistent high-risk HPV infection.

live_plab_copy.stem: A pregnant woman asks about screening for Down syndrome.  What does antenatal screening primarily provide?

options.A: An estimate of the likelihood of the condition
options.B: A prediction of the child's adult height
options.C: Confirmation that the fetus is genetically normal
options.E: A definite diagnosis in every case

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. An estimate of the likelihood of the condition
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Screening estimates the likelihood of a condition; diagnostic testing is required when a definitive diagnosis is needed.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Screening does not predict adult height. C. A low-risk screening result does not guarantee that the fetus is     unaffected. D. Screening does not treat the condition. E. Screening is not diagnostic.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Antenatal screening tests (such as combined or quadruple testing) give a risk estimate, while a definitive diagnosis of a chromosomal condition requires an invasive diagnostic test such as chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis.
live_plab_copy.thinking: A question about what screening 'provides' is testing the screening-versus-diagnostic distinction, so the answer must be a probability or likelihood, not a confirmed yes/no result.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: Conflating a low-risk screening result with a guarantee the fetus is unaffected, when screening by definition cannot provide that certainty.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Antenatal screening estimates risk; only a diagnostic test like amniocentesis confirms the diagnosis.

live_plab_copy.stem: Which vaccine type is generally avoided during pregnancy because it contains live attenuated organisms?

options.A: Live attenuated vaccine

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Live attenuated vaccine
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Live attenuated vaccines are generally avoided during pregnancy as a precaution because of theoretical fetal risk.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Toxoid vaccines use inactivated toxins. C. Inactivated vaccines do not contain replicating live organisms. D. Recombinant subunit vaccines contain selected antigenic components. E. Conjugate vaccines contain antigen linked to a carrier protein.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Live vaccines such as MMR, varicella and BCG are generally avoided in pregnancy; inactivated, toxoid and subunit vaccines can be given when indicated.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnancy ↓ Concern is a vaccine organism that can replicate ↓ Only live attenuated vaccines contain replicating organisms ↓ Live attenuated vaccine
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, toxoid vaccine — 'toxin' sounds risky in pregnancy, but toxoids are inactivated toxins that cannot replicate and are not routinely avoided.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: In pregnancy avoid live vaccines; inactivated vaccines are generally acceptable.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: A very painful swelling at the vaginal opening is a Bartholin abscess.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 51-year-old woman has hot flushes, night sweats and irregular periods. Her symptoms are affecting her quality of life.

Which is the most appropriate general approach?

options.A: Arrange FSH testing to confirm menopause before any treatment
options.B: Discuss options, including menopausal hormone therapy
options.C: Advise that symptoms should be tolerated until periods stop
options.E: Refer for hysterectomy and bilateral oophorectomy

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Discuss options, including menopausal hormone therapy
live_plab_copy.why_correct: NICE NG23 recommends discussing management options for menopausal symptoms affecting quality of life, with HRT the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms after individual benefits and risks are considered.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. FSH testing is not needed to diagnose perimenopause in women over 45 with typical symptoms. C. Effective treatments are available and symptoms affecting quality of life should be managed. D. Non-hormonal options are not first line; HRT is most effective for vasomotor symptoms. E. Surgery is not indicated for menopausal symptoms.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Over 45 with typical vasomotor symptoms, perimenopause is a clinical diagnosis without FSH testing; HRT is the most effective treatment, discussed with individual benefits and risks.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Woman aged 51 ↓ hot flushes, night sweats and irregular periods ↓ clinical diagnosis of perimenopause ↓ symptoms affect quality of life ↓ discuss options, including menopausal hormone therapy
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, FSH testing before any treatment — tempting as objective confirmation, but it is unnecessary over 45 with typical symptoms, and levels fluctuate in perimenopause.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Perimenopause over 45 is a clinical diagnosis; HRT is the most effective symptom treatment.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, serum progesterone alone — a pregnancy-related blood test, but it does not establish gestational age.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Date pregnancies by ultrasound, especially when the LMP is uncertain.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman at term is found to have a persistent breech presentation.

Which principle is appropriate?

options.A: Discuss management options, taking account of her preferences
options.B: Book a planned caesarean section without discussing other options
options.C: Offer external cephalic version once labour has started
options.D: Arrange an immediate caesarean section on the day of diagnosis
options.E: Await spontaneous labour and plan a vaginal birth as usual

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Discuss management options, taking account of her preferences
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Persistent breech presentation at term requires discussion of options, including external cephalic version, planned caesarean section or planned vaginal breech birth, considering gestation, maternal and fetal factors and patient preference (RCOG Green-top Guideline 20b and NICE NG192).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Options such as external cephalic version should be discussed. C. External cephalic version is offered before labour, not during it. D. Breech at diagnosis does not mandate immediate caesarean section. E. Breech presentation significantly influences delivery planning.
live_plab_copy.pearl: For breech at term, offer external cephalic version to suitable women; if declined or unsuccessful, discuss planned caesarean birth and vaginal breech birth so she can make an informed choice.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Persistent breech at term ↓ several reasonable options exist ↓ ECV, planned caesarean or vaginal breech birth ↓ choice depends on clinical factors and her preference ↓ discuss options with her
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, book a caesarean without discussing other options — tempting as a common outcome for breech, but it ignores ECV and her right to an informed choice.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Breech at term: discuss ECV and birth options and let the woman make an informed choice.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A pregnant woman has been exposed to someone with suspected rubella.

What is the most appropriate principle?

options.A: Arrange urgent assessment because rubella can harm the fetus
options.B: Offer termination of pregnancy on the basis of the exposure
options.C: Reassure her, as fetal harm occurs in late pregnancy
options.E: Give a dose of MMR vaccine now to protect the pregnancy

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Arrange urgent assessment because rubella can harm the fetus
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Maternal rubella infection can cause congenital rubella syndrome, so suspected exposure requires appropriate assessment. Live vaccines such as MMR are not routinely given during pregnancy.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Exposure alone does not justify termination; immunity and infection must be assessed first. C. Fetal risk from rubella is greatest in early pregnancy, not late pregnancy, so this reassurance is wrong. D. Rubella is viral, so antibiotics have no role. E. MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Rubella is most dangerous to the fetus in early pregnancy; after exposure, check immunity and test for infection promptly. MMR is live and must not be given during pregnancy.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant woman exposed to suspected rubella ↓ Risk of congenital rubella syndrome, greatest early in pregnancy ↓ Needs prompt immunity check and testing ↓ A, urgent assessment
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, MMR now — tempting as a protective step, but MMR is a live vaccine contraindicated in pregnancy; non-immune women are offered it after delivery.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Rubella contact in pregnancy means prompt assessment; never give live vaccines during pregnancy.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: UTI in pregnancy always needs treatment and a urine culture.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman is offered a screening test for a fetal chromosomal condition. She asks whether a positive result proves that the fetus has the condition. What is the correct explanation?

options.E: No; but a detailed anomaly scan at 20 weeks will confirm it

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. No; it estimates risk; diagnostic testing may follow
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Screening estimates the probability of a condition; diagnostic testing is used when definitive confirmation is required.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Repeating a screening test does not provide a diagnosis. C. A higher-chance result estimates probability and does not confirm the diagnosis. D. Screening is not equivalent to diagnosis and false-positive results occur. E. Ultrasound findings can support suspicion but do not confirm a chromosomal diagnosis; diagnostic testing such as CVS or amniocentesis is required.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Antenatal screening for chromosomal conditions gives a chance estimate; a higher-chance result leads to an offer of further testing, with CVS or amniocentesis needed for a diagnosis.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant woman offered screening ↓ Screening estimates chance, not certainty ↓ False positives occur ↓ No; it estimates risk; diagnostic testing may follow
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, the 20-week anomaly scan will confirm it — ultrasound markers can raise suspicion, but only invasive testing such as CVS or amniocentesis confirms a chromosomal diagnosis.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Screening gives a chance; CVS or amniocentesis gives a diagnosis.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Abnormal cervical cells mean possible precancer needing follow-up, not cancer.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Smokers aged 35 or over should generally avoid combined hormonal contraception.

live_plab_copy.why_correct: A previous ectopic pregnancy is an established risk factor for another ectopic pregnancy.
