live_plab_copy.thinking: Previous ectopic pregnancy ↓ Tubal damage or underlying risk persists ↓ Higher chance of recurrence ↓ Previous ectopic pregnancy increases recurrence risk
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, ectopic pregnancy only with fibroids — it names a plausible gynaecological condition, but ectopic risk relates mainly to tubal damage, and 'only' makes it false.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: A past ectopic raises recurrence risk: confirm the pregnancy site early next time.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman with suspected eclampsia has a seizure.

What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Give IV diazepam first-line and await the obstetric team
options.B: Give IV phenytoin as the first-line anticonvulsant
options.C: Proceed to immediate caesarean section during the seizure
options.D: Arrange an urgent CT head before giving any treatment
options.E: Call for help, stabilise and give IV magnesium sulfate

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Call for help, stabilise and give IV magnesium sulfate
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Eclampsia is an obstetric emergency: call for help, support the airway and breathing, place the woman in left lateral tilt, give IV magnesium sulfate to treat and prevent seizures, control blood pressure and plan delivery once stabilised (NICE NG133).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Magnesium sulfate, not diazepam, is the first-line anticonvulsant in eclampsia. B. Phenytoin is less effective than magnesium sulfate in eclampsia. C. The woman must be stabilised before delivery is planned. D. Imaging must not delay emergency treatment with magnesium sulfate.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Magnesium sulfate is the anticonvulsant of choice in eclampsia, both to stop the seizure and to prevent recurrence; call for help, protect the airway and use left lateral tilt.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Suspected eclampsia with a seizure ↓ Obstetric emergency: call for help, ABC, left lateral tilt ↓ Magnesium sulfate treats and prevents eclamptic seizures ↓ Call for help, stabilise and give IV magnesium sulfate
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, IV diazepam first-line — benzodiazepines are the reflex for seizures elsewhere, but in eclampsia magnesium sulfate is more effective and is the first-line treatment.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Eclamptic seizure: call for help, stabilise and give magnesium sulfate; plan delivery only once stable.

A pregnant woman develops dysuria and urinary frequency.

Why is prompt assessment and management important?

options.A: Pregnancy raises the risk of UTI complications

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Dysuria should not be attributed to candidiasis without assessment for UTI. C. UTI is not a common cause of pre-eclampsia. D. Pregnancy does not reduce antibiotic effectiveness. E. Urinary symptoms are not a sign of miscarriage.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Ureteric dilatation and urinary stasis in pregnancy make ascending infection and pyelonephritis more likely, so UTI in pregnancy needs a urine culture and prompt pregnancy-safe antibiotics.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant with dysuria and frequency ↓ Pregnancy causes ureteric dilatation and stasis ↓ Infection ascends more readily, with maternal and fetal consequences ↓ Pregnancy raises the risk of UTI complications
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, UTI as a common cause of pre-eclampsia — sounds like a plausible pregnancy complication, but pre-eclampsia is placental in origin, not caused by UTI.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Treat UTI in pregnancy promptly; it ascends easily to pyelonephritis.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Rash exposure in pregnancy: check immunity first and seek specialist advice.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 38-year-old woman who smokes 20 cigarettes a day asks for the combined oral contraceptive pill.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Prescribe the combined pill, provided her blood pressure and BMI are within normal range
options.B: Prescribe a low-dose 20 microgram combined pill with annual review
options.C: Prescribe the combined transdermal patch, as it carries a lower arterial risk than the pill
options.D: Do not use combined hormonal contraception (UKMEC 4); offer a non-oestrogen method
options.E: Prescribe the combined pill provided she cuts down to 10 cigarettes a day

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Do not use combined hormonal contraception (UKMEC 4); offer a non-oestrogen method
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Under the UK Medical Eligibility Criteria, a woman aged 35 or over who smokes 15 or more cigarettes a day is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception (an unacceptable health risk) because of the increased risk of arterial thrombosis. She should be offered a non-oestrogen method, such as LARC or a progestogen-only method, together with smoking cessation support. Source: FSRH UK Medical Eligibility Criteria.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Normal blood pressure and BMI do not offset the risk: age 35 or over with 15 or more cigarettes a day is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception regardless. B. A lower oestrogen dose does not change the UKMEC 4 category for combined hormonal contraception. C. The patch is combined hormonal contraception and carries the same UKMEC 4 category; it is not safer. E. She currently smokes 20 a day, and even reduced smoking at her age is UKMEC 3, so a non-oestrogen method remains preferable.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Contraception questions are often eligibility questions, not "which pill is best?" questions.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Combined hormonal contraception  ↓  assess VTE/cardiovascular risk factors.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, a low-dose 20 microgram pill — less oestrogen seems safer, but the category is unchanged: age 35 or over smoking 15 or more a day is UKMEC 4.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Age 35 or over and smoking 15 or more a day: combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC 4.

live_plab_copy.stem: A woman with PMOS (formerly PCOS) is found to have obesity and insulin resistance. Which long-term condition is she at increased risk of developing?

options.A: Addisonian crisis

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Type 2 diabetes mellitus

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Addisonian crisis results from adrenal insufficiency. B. Hypoparathyroidism causes hypocalcaemia and is not linked to PMOS (formerly PCOS). C. Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune and is not caused by insulin resistance or PMOS (formerly PCOS). E. Diabetes insipidus is due to ADH deficiency or resistance and is unrelated to insulin resistance.
live_plab_copy.pearl: PMOS (formerly PCOS) carries an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, especially with obesity; offer regular glycaemic screening and weight-management support.
live_plab_copy.thinking: PMOS (formerly PCOS) ↓ Obesity ↓ Insulin resistance ↓ Impaired glucose tolerance over time ↓ Type 2 diabetes mellitus
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, type 1 diabetes — diabetes is the right theme, which tempts, but type 1 is autoimmune beta-cell destruction and is not driven by insulin resistance.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: PMOS (formerly PCOS) with obesity raises the risk of type 2 diabetes.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A pregnant woman asks whether seasonal influenza vaccination is appropriate.

Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Influenza vaccination is recommended during pregnancy
options.C: Only women with diabetes should be vaccinated
options.D: All vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy
options.E: Vaccination must always be delayed until after delivery

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Influenza vaccination is recommended during pregnancy
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Seasonal influenza vaccination is offered during pregnancy because pregnant women have increased risk of complications from influenza and vaccination also provides protection to the infant after birth.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. The recommended influenza vaccines do not cause influenza infection. C. The recommendation is not restricted to women with diabetes. D. Some vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy, but not all. E. Vaccination should not routinely be postponed until after delivery.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Inactivated influenza vaccine is offered to all pregnant women during flu season at any stage of pregnancy; it protects the mother and passes antibodies that protect the baby in early infancy.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant woman asks about flu vaccine ↓ Pregnancy raises the risk of severe influenza ↓ Inactivated vaccine is safe at any gestation ↓ Vaccination is recommended during pregnancy
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, all vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy — tempting caution, but only live vaccines are avoided; inactivated influenza vaccine is actively recommended.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Offer inactivated flu vaccine to every pregnant woman in flu season.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman requests emergency contraception after unprotected intercourse.

What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Offer levonorgestrel if within 24 hours, otherwise decline
options.B: Assess timing and offer emergency contraception promptly
options.C: Arrange a pregnancy test first and offer EC if it is negative
options.D: Advise waiting for the next period before deciding on EC
options.E: Offer a copper IUD at the next routine clinic in four weeks

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Assess timing and offer emergency contraception promptly
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Emergency contraception should be offered promptly after assessing timing and cycle, with options including the copper IUD (most effective) or oral levonorgestrel or ulipristal acetate, following FSRH guidance.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Levonorgestrel can be used up to 72 hours, ulipristal up to 120 hours and a copper IUD up to 5 days, so presenting after 24 hours does not exclude emergency contraception. C. A pregnancy test cannot detect a pregnancy from this episode so soon and should not delay emergency contraception. D. Waiting for a period loses the window for emergency contraception. E. A copper IUD for emergency contraception must be fitted within 5 days of intercourse or of the earliest expected ovulation.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Emergency contraception should be offered promptly; the copper IUD is most effective, and oral ulipristal acetate or levonorgestrel are options depending on timing and circumstances.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Unprotected intercourse ↓ Request for emergency contraception ↓ Effectiveness falls with delay ↓ Assess timing and offer emergency contraception promptly
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, a pregnancy test first — it seems prudent, but it cannot detect a pregnancy from this episode so soon and only delays effective treatment.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Emergency contraception: assess timing and offer it promptly; do not delay for tests.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 62-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding three years after her last menstrual period. She does not take hormone replacement therapy.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Trial topical vaginal oestrogen and refer if the bleeding recurs
options.B: Arrange a routine gynaecology appointment within 18 weeks
options.C: Refer on the suspected cancer pathway for endometrial assessment
options.D: Repeat cervical screening and refer if the result is abnormal
options.E: Prescribe tranexamic acid and review in three months

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Refer on the suspected cancer pathway for endometrial assessment
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Postmenopausal bleeding needs assessment for endometrial cancer; NICE NG12 (updated 2026) recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for women aged 55 or over with unexplained postmenopausal bleeding that cannot be attributed to hormone replacement therapy (HRT), with transvaginal ultrasound and further investigation as indicated.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Atrophy cannot be assumed; postmenopausal bleeding needs urgent assessment for endometrial cancer. B. A routine referral delays diagnosis; NICE NG12 recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for women aged 55 or over with unexplained postmenopausal bleeding not attributable to HRT. D. Cervical screening does not assess the endometrium. E. Tranexamic acid treats the symptom and delays investigation for malignancy.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Unexplained postmenopausal bleeding not attributable to HRT in a woman aged 55 or over warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral to exclude endometrial cancer.
live_plab_copy.thinking: 62-year-old woman ↓ Vaginal bleeding three years after menopause ↓ Not taking HRT ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral for endometrial assessment
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, vaginal oestrogen for presumed atrophy — atrophy is common, but it cannot be assumed; endometrial cancer must be excluded first.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Postmenopausal bleeding not explained by HRT: suspected cancer pathway referral.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman with PMOS (formerly PCOS) has excess facial hair and acne.

Which hormone group is primarily responsible for these clinical features?

options.A: Androgens

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Androgens
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Hyperandrogenism, from increased ovarian androgen production and reduced sex hormone-binding globulin, causes hirsutism and acne in PMOS (formerly PCOS).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Thyroid hormone abnormalities are not the mechanism of hirsutism and acne in PMOS (formerly PCOS). C. Prolactin deficiency does not cause hirsutism or acne. D. Cortisol deficiency causes adrenal insufficiency rather than the androgenic features of PMOS (formerly PCOS). E. Oestrogens do not cause hirsutism or acne; these are androgenic features.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Hirsutism and acne in PMOS (formerly PCOS) reflect hyperandrogenism from raised ovarian androgens and low SHBG; insulin resistance contributes, so weight reduction can improve symptoms.
live_plab_copy.thinking: PMOS (formerly PCOS) ↓ Excess facial hair and acne ↓ Both are androgen-dependent features ↓ Raised ovarian androgens and low SHBG ↓ Androgens
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, oestrogens only — ovarian hormones are the obvious guess, but oestrogens do not cause hirsutism or acne; these signs come from androgen excess.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Hirsutism and acne mean androgen excess; in PMOS it is ovarian hyperandrogenism.

live_plab_copy.stem:
At term, a fetus is found to be in a persistent breech presentation.

What should this prompt?

options.A: Planned caesarean section at 39 weeks without discussing other options
options.B: Induction of labour at 37 weeks to allow a planned vaginal breech birth
options.C: Repeat ultrasound at 41 weeks, as most breech babies turn spontaneously
options.D: Discussion of options, including external cephalic version if suitable
options.E: Emergency caesarean section on the same day, before labour starts

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Discussion of options, including external cephalic version if suitable
live_plab_copy.why_correct: NICE NG201 advises offering external cephalic version to women with an uncomplicated breech at 36 weeks or later, alongside discussion of vaginal breech birth and planned caesarean.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Caesarean is an option, but the woman should be offered a discussion of all options, including ECV. B. Induction is not the routine response to breech presentation. C. Spontaneous version becomes less likely at term, and waiting delays discussion of ECV and birth planning. E. An uncomplicated breech at term is not an emergency and does not need same-day caesarean.
live_plab_copy.pearl: For an uncomplicated breech at term, offer external cephalic version if suitable and discuss planned caesarean and vaginal breech birth, so the woman can make an informed choice.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Term pregnancy ↓ Persistent breech presentation ↓ Several reasonable birth options ↓ ECV may turn the baby if suitable ↓ Discussion of options, including external cephalic version if suitable
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, planned caesarean at 39 weeks without discussing options — tempting as caesarean is a common route. It skips informed choice and ECV, which may allow a vaginal birth.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Term breech: offer ECV if suitable and discuss all birth options.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman of reproductive age presents with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding.

Which investigation is particularly important early in the assessment?

options.A: Spirometry

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Pregnancy testing
live_plab_copy.why_correct: In any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding, a pregnancy test is essential early because ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage must be considered, and pregnancy status changes investigation and management (NICE NG126).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Spirometry assesses lung function and is irrelevant here. C. Serum cholesterol does not help assess an acute gynaecological or pregnancy-related presentation. D. Bone-density scanning has no role in acute abdominal pain with bleeding. E. Hearing assessment is unrelated to this presentation.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding needs an early pregnancy test, because ectopic pregnancy must be excluded even when pregnancy seems unlikely.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnancy status can fundamentally alter the differential diagnosis and management of abdominal or pelvic symptoms.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, serum cholesterol — tempting only as a routine blood test, but it has no role in an acute presentation where ectopic pregnancy must be excluded.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Reproductive-age woman with pain and bleeding: pregnancy test early.

A 47-year-old woman has increasingly heavy periods and bleeding between periods. Pregnancy testing is negative.

What is the most appropriate principle of management?

options.A: Prescribe antibiotics for presumed endometritis and review
options.B: Reassure her and review if bleeding continues
options.C: Attribute it to the perimenopause and observe
options.D: Investigate for the cause of her abnormal bleeding
options.E: Start the combined pill to regulate her cycle

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Investigate for the cause of her abnormal bleeding
live_plab_copy.why_correct: New or changing abnormal uterine bleeding requires assessment for structural, hormonal and other causes, including significant pathology.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of infection. B. New intermenstrual or increasingly heavy bleeding should be assessed rather than observed. C. Perimenopause can alter bleeding patterns but should not explain new abnormal bleeding without assessment. E. Hormonal treatment should not be started before the cause has been assessed.
live_plab_copy.pearl: New intermenstrual or worsening heavy bleeding needs examination and investigation, which may include pelvic ultrasound and endometrial sampling, before it is blamed on age.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Woman in her late forties ↓ Increasingly heavy periods ↓ New intermenstrual bleeding ↓ Pregnancy excluded ↓ Investigate for the cause of her abnormal bleeding
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, attribute it to the perimenopause — her age makes cycle change plausible, but new intermenstrual bleeding must be investigated before blaming hormones.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: New abnormal uterine bleeding needs investigation, not attribution to age.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A pregnant woman develops dysuria and urinary frequency. She has no flank pain or systemic symptoms.

What is the most appropriate general approach?

options.A: Treat suspected urinary tract infection promptly
options.B: Ignore the symptoms because urinary frequency is normal in pregnancy
options.C: Wait until after delivery before testing

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Treat suspected urinary tract infection promptly
live_plab_copy.why_correct: UTIs in pregnancy require appropriate assessment and treatment because untreated infection can progress to complications including pyelonephritis.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Although urinary frequency can be physiological, dysuria suggests infection and should not simply be ignored. C. Treatment should not be unnecessarily delayed until delivery. D. Renal biopsy is not indicated for uncomplicated suspected UTI. E. Fluid restriction is inappropriate.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Lower UTI in pregnancy should always be treated: send a urine culture before starting antibiotics, choose a pregnancy-safe agent, and avoid trimethoprim in the first trimester.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Dysuria and frequency suggest lower UTI ↓ No flank pain or systemic features ↓ Untreated UTI in pregnancy can progress to pyelonephritis ↓ Treat suspected UTI promptly
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, ignore the symptoms — frequency is common in pregnancy and tempts reassurance, but dysuria is not physiological and untreated infection risks pyelonephritis.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Any UTI in pregnancy: culture and treat promptly; never dismiss it as pregnancy frequency.

akt_source.why_wrong: B. Although urinary frequency can be physiological, dysuria suggests infection and should not simply be ignored. C. Treatment should not be unnecessarily delayed until delivery. D. Renal biopsy is not indicated for uncomplicated suspected UTI. E. Fluid restriction is inappropriate.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 38-year-old who smokes asks about starting combined hormonal contraception.

What is important?

options.A: Smoking matters only if she also has a BMI above 35 kg/m²
options.B: Combined hormonal contraception is suitable if she has smoked for under 10 years
options.C: Smoking reduces the efficacy of combined contraception, so condoms are needed
options.D: Combined hormonal contraception is unrestricted until 40 years of age
options.E: Assess smoking and other risks, as risks of combined methods rise with age

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Assess smoking and other risks, as risks of combined methods rise with age
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Under UKMEC, combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC 3 for smokers aged 35 or over who smoke fewer than 15 cigarettes daily and UKMEC 4 for 15 or more daily, so age and smoking must be assessed.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Smoking at 35 or over is itself a significant risk factor with combined hormonal contraception, regardless of BMI. B. UKMEC categories for smokers depend on age and current smoking, not on the duration of smoking. C. Smoking does not make contraception less effective; it increases the cardiovascular risks of oestrogen. D. From age 35, smoking makes combined hormonal contraception UKMEC 3 or 4, so it is not unrestricted.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Combined hormonal contraception carries arterial and venous risks that rise with age and smoking. From 35, smoking makes combined methods UKMEC 3 or 4, so assess smoking and other risks before prescribing.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Age 38 ↓ Current smoker ↓ Oestrogen adds to age- and smoking-related cardiovascular risk ↓ UKMEC restricts combined methods ↓ Assess smoking and other risks, as risks of combined methods rise with age
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, unrestricted until 40 years of age — tempting because 40 is a familiar contraception age. From 35, smoking alone makes combined methods UKMEC 3 or 4.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Smoker aged 35 or over: combined methods are usually avoided; consider progestogen-only or non-hormonal.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 29-year-old woman with a positive pregnancy test presents with unilateral lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. She becomes pale and hypotensive.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Measure serum hCG and repeat it in 48 hours before deciding on care
options.B: Treat as possible ruptured ectopic; arrange emergency assessment
options.C: Refer to the early pregnancy unit for a scan the next working day
options.D: Give oral ferrous sulfate for anaemia and review her in one month
options.E: Wait for her routine booking antenatal appointment with the midwife

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Treat as possible ruptured ectopic; arrange emergency assessment
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Early pregnancy with pain, bleeding and haemodynamic instability raises immediate concern for ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Source: NICE NG126, Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Serial hCG is for stable women with a pregnancy of unknown location; it delays care in an unstable patient. C. Haemodynamic instability requires immediate emergency assessment, not a next-day scan. D. Iron does not address the acute problem. E. Emergency assessment is required, not a routine antenatal appointment.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In pregnancy, clinical condition takes priority over an isolated hCG result.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Early pregnancy + pain/bleeding + instability  ↓  ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, serial hCG over 48 hours — correct for a stable pregnancy of unknown location, but unsafe once she is pale and hypotensive with suspected rupture.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Positive pregnancy test, pain and shock: ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise, needing emergency assessment.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A postmenopausal woman has persistent itching and a new irregular lesion on the vulva.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Advise review if the lesion becomes painful or bleeds
options.B: Reassure and discharge with a soap substitute and emollients
options.C: Arrange assessment of the persistent vulval lesion
options.D: Prescribe topical clotrimazole for presumed candidiasis
options.E: Treat with a course of oral antibiotics without examination

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Arrange assessment of the persistent vulval lesion
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Persistent vulval symptoms or an unexplained lesion can be features of vulval cancer and require assessment.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Vulval cancer is often painless in its early stages, so waiting for pain or bleeding is unsafe. B. A persistent vulval lesion in a postmenopausal woman warrants assessment under NICE NG12, not discharge with emollients. D. Candidiasis should not be presumed and treated in the presence of a new irregular lesion, which raises concern for vulval cancer. E. There is no evidence of bacterial infection, and antibiotics without examination would delay diagnosis of a possible malignancy.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Persistent vulval itch with a new irregular lesion in a postmenopausal woman raises concern for vulval cancer; examine and refer for assessment rather than treat empirically.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Postmenopausal woman ↓ Persistent vulval itch ↓ New irregular lesion ↓ Possible vulval cancer ↓ C, arrange assessment
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, clotrimazole for candidiasis — tempting because itch suggests thrush, but a new irregular lesion must be examined, not treated blindly.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: A persistent or irregular vulval lesion needs examination, not empirical treatment.

live_plab_copy.stem: A woman has had unprotected sexual intercourse and does not wish to become pregnant. What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Consider emergency contraception promptly
options.D: Emergency contraception is ineffective after any unprotected intercourse
options.E: Wait until the next menstrual period before considering it

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Consider emergency contraception promptly
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Emergency contraception should be considered as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse, with the appropriate method chosen according to timing and circumstances.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Antibiotics do not prevent pregnancy. C. Insulin has no role. D. Emergency contraception has recognised indications after unprotected intercourse. E. Waiting may reduce available options and effectiveness.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Emergency contraception options are the copper IUD (most effective), ulipristal and levonorgestrel; offer it as soon as possible, choosing the method by timing and circumstances.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Unprotected intercourse ↓ Pregnancy not wanted ↓ Effectiveness falls with delay ↓ Consider emergency contraception promptly
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, waiting until the next period — may seem sensible to see whether pregnancy occurs, but delay narrows the options and reduces effectiveness; act promptly.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Offer emergency contraception as soon as possible after unprotected sex.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient taking a combined oral contraceptive pill has missed pills. What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Stop the pill and rely on condoms until the next period starts
options.B: Take two pills each day for the remainder of the pack to catch up
options.C: It depends on how many pills were missed and when in the pack
options.D: Emergency contraception is needed after one missed pill
options.E: No further action is needed if fewer than three pills were missed

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. It depends on how many pills were missed and when in the pack
live_plab_copy.why_correct: The need for additional precautions or emergency contraception depends on the specific circumstances of the missed pills.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Stopping the pill is unnecessary and leaves the patient unprotected. B. Doubling doses for the rest of the pack is not recommended. D. Emergency contraception is not automatically required after one missed pill. E. Missing two or more pills can require additional precautions and possibly emergency contraception.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Missed combined pill advice depends on how many pills were missed and where in the pack; one missed pill usually needs only taking it now, while more may need extra precautions or emergency contraception.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Combined oral contraceptive ↓ Missed pills ↓ Risk depends on number missed and week of pack ↓ Determines need for condoms or emergency contraception ↓ It depends on how many and when
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, No action if fewer than three missed — it sounds like a familiar rule, but missing two or more pills can require extra precautions and possibly emergency contraception.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Missed pill advice hinges on how many were missed and where in the pack.

A cervical screening sample shows abnormal cervical cells that require further assessment.

What is the significance of these changes?

options.A: They confirm pelvic inflammatory disease

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. They may represent precancerous changes
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Abnormal cervical cells can represent precancerous changes requiring appropriate follow-up and management.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Cervical cell abnormalities do not diagnose PID. C. They do not establish infertility. D. They are unrelated to ectopic pregnancy. E. Abnormal cells do not automatically mean invasive cancer.

live_plab_copy.thinking: Abnormal cervical cells ↓ Screening detects precancer before cancer ↓ Further assessment at colposcopy ↓ May represent precancerous changes
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, confirm invasive cervical cancer — abnormal cells sound serious, but most are precancerous and only histology can confirm invasion.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Abnormal screening cells usually mean treatable precancer, not cancer.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman undergoing assisted reproductive treatment develops abdominal pain, bloating and rapidly increasing abdominal distension.

Which complication should be considered?

options.A: Vulvovaginal candidiasis with discharge

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome can cause enlarged ovaries, abdominal distension and fluid shifts following ovarian stimulation.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Vulvovaginal candidiasis causes vulval itching and discharge, not abdominal distension. B. Menopause does not cause acute abdominal pain and distension. D. IBS can cause bloating but does not cause rapidly increasing abdominal distension after ovarian stimulation. E. Endometriosis causes chronic cyclical pelvic pain and does not cause rapidly increasing distension after ovarian stimulation.
live_plab_copy.pearl: OHSS follows ovarian stimulation, causing enlarged ovaries and fluid shifts; severe cases bring ascites, haemoconcentration and thrombosis risk, needing urgent specialist assessment.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Assisted reproductive treatment ↓ Ovarian stimulation ↓ Abdominal pain, bloating, rapid distension ↓ Fluid shift into third space ↓ C, OHSS
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, IBS exacerbation — tempting because bloating is prominent, but IBS does not cause rapidly increasing distension after ovarian stimulation.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Abdominal distension after fertility treatment: think ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman develops heavy vaginal bleeding shortly after delivery and becomes tachycardic and hypotensive.

What is the priority?

options.A: Oral iron and a repeat full blood count in one week
options.B: Reassure her that some bleeding is expected after delivery
options.C: Observe on the postnatal ward with routine observations
options.D: Immediate assessment and management of postpartum haemorrhage
options.E: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound at the routine postnatal review

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Immediate assessment and management of postpartum haemorrhage
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Heavy bleeding with tachycardia and hypotension after delivery is postpartum haemorrhage with shock, which needs immediate resuscitation and management of the cause.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Oral iron does not treat acute haemorrhage or shock. B. Heavy bleeding with tachycardia and hypotension is not normal and needs immediate action. C. Routine observations would delay treatment of haemorrhagic shock. E. Waiting for routine review would delay life-saving treatment.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Postpartum tachycardia and hypotension mean significant blood loss: call for help, resuscitate and treat the cause using the 4 Ts (tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin), with uterine atony the commonest.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Shortly after delivery ↓ Heavy vaginal bleeding ↓ Tachycardia and hypotension ↓ Haemorrhagic shock ↓ Immediate assessment and management of postpartum haemorrhage
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, some bleeding is expected after delivery — tempting because lochia is normal. Heavy bleeding with tachycardia and hypotension is haemorrhage with shock, not normal loss.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Heavy postpartum bleeding with shock: call for help, resuscitate and treat the 4 Ts.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 35-year-old pregnant woman develops sudden vaginal bleeding with severe abdominal pain and becomes hypotensive. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Perform a vaginal examination to assess the cervix
options.B: ABCDE assessment and resuscitation of the mother
options.C: Start continuous CTG monitoring before other steps
options.D: Give oral analgesia and reassess in an hour
options.E: Arrange an ultrasound scan in the antenatal clinic

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. ABCDE assessment and resuscitation of the mother
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Maternal haemodynamic compromise is an emergency; immediate resuscitation and stabilisation take priority.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Vaginal examination does not address maternal shock and may be dangerous if placenta praevia is present. C. Fetal monitoring must not delay maternal resuscitation. D. Oral analgesia and delayed review are unsafe in a hypotensive patient. E. A clinic scan would delay emergency resuscitation.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In antepartum haemorrhage with shock, resuscitate the mother first with ABCDE, large-bore access and blood; maternal stabilisation is also the best treatment for the fetus.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant woman with sudden bleeding and severe pain ↓ Hypotension indicates haemorrhagic shock ↓ Mother's life is the priority ↓ ABCDE assessment and resuscitation
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, continuous CTG monitoring — fetal wellbeing matters, which tempts, but monitoring must never delay resuscitation of a shocked mother.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Shocked pregnant woman: resuscitate the mother first.

A pregnant woman presents with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain. She is RhD-negative.

Which principle is important?

options.A: Give anti-D for any bleeding, irrespective of gestation or cause
options.B: Assess the need for anti-D according to the clinical situation
options.C: Give anti-D first, as this makes further investigation unnecessary
options.D: Give anti-D and defer assessment for ectopic pregnancy to clinic
options.E: Withhold anti-D until the partner's RhD status has been checked

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Assess the need for anti-D according to the clinical situation
live_plab_copy.why_correct: RhD-negative women with bleeding or pregnancy complications require assessment according to current anti-D recommendations. This does not replace assessment of the underlying cause. Source: NICE NG126, Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage.

Anti-D does not diagnose or treat ectopic pregnancy, which needs prompt assessment. E. Waiting for partner testing is not the standard approach and may delay indicated prophylaxis.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Do not let a prophylactic intervention distract from the primary diagnosis.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Early pregnancy bleeding + RhD-negative  ↓  consider anti-D guidance and investigate the cause.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, anti-D for any bleeding — it feels protective, but eligibility depends on gestation and circumstances, and the cause of bleeding still needs assessment.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: RhD-negative with bleeding: decide on anti-D by gestation and situation, and still find the cause.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, send culture and await the result — seems prudent, but delaying treatment in a symptomatic pregnant woman risks pyelonephritis.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: UTI in pregnancy: send culture and start antibiotics straight away.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Prompt maternity assessment
options.D: Wait until the next routine antenatal appointment

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Prompt maternity assessment
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Significantly reduced fetal movements after 24 weeks may indicate fetal compromise. The woman should contact her maternity unit immediately and be assessed promptly, including CTG monitoring (RCOG Green-top Guideline 57).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. A cervical smear is irrelevant and is usually deferred until after pregnancy. C. Antibiotics are not indicated for reduced fetal movements. D. live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman at 9 weeks' gestation has mild vaginal spotting. Her cervical os is closed. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an intrauterine pregnancy with a crown–rump length of 12 mm and no fetal cardiac activity, confirmed by a second sonographer.

Which diagnosis is most consistent?

options.A: Ectopic pregnancy

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Missed miscarriage
live_plab_copy.why_correct: With a closed os, minimal bleeding and an intrauterine pregnancy with CRL of 7 mm or more and no fetal heartbeat confirmed by a second opinion, the criteria for a missed (delayed) miscarriage are met (NICE NG126). The products of conception are retained without expulsion.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. The ultrasound confirms an intrauterine pregnancy, which makes ectopic pregnancy very unlikely. B. Hyperemesis gravidarum causes severe vomiting, not vaginal bleeding with a non-viable pregnancy. C. Placental abruption is a complication of later pregnancy, after 20 weeks. E. Pre-eclampsia occurs after 20 weeks and presents with hypertension and proteinuria, not first-trimester bleeding.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Missed miscarriage is often painless with little bleeding and a closed os; diagnosis rests on an intrauterine pregnancy with no heartbeat at an adequate crown–rump length, confirmed by a second opinion.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Mild spotting with a closed os ↓ intrauterine pregnancy on scan ↓ CRL above the diagnostic threshold ↓ no cardiac activity, confirmed by a second sonographer ↓ missed miscarriage
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, ectopic pregnancy — tempting because of first-trimester bleeding, but the scan confirms an intrauterine pregnancy, making ectopic pregnancy very unlikely.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Closed os, intrauterine pregnancy, no heartbeat at adequate CRL: missed miscarriage.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 32-year-old woman receives an invitation for routine cervical screening. She has no symptoms. What is the primary purpose of cervical screening?

options.A: Detect high-risk HPV and precancerous cervical changes
options.B: Diagnose cervical cancer in symptomatic women
options.C: Detect early endometrial cancer in asymptomatic women
options.D: Detect ovarian cancer at an early stage
options.E: Screen for chlamydia and other sexually transmitted infections

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Detect high-risk HPV and precancerous cervical changes
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Cervical screening aims to identify high-risk HPV and associated cellular abnormalities so that precancerous changes can be managed before invasive cancer develops.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Symptomatic women require diagnostic assessment rather than relying on screening. C. Cervical screening does not screen for endometrial cancer. D. Cervical screening does not screen for ovarian cancer. E. Cervical screening is not a test for chlamydia or other STIs.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Cervical screening is designed to detect high-risk HPV and pre-cancerous cervical changes in asymptomatic women, not to diagnose established cancer or unrelated gynaecological conditions.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Separate screening (asymptomatic population, aims to catch disease early) from diagnostic testing (symptomatic individual), then match the option that reflects prevention rather than diagnosis.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: Candidates may conflate cervical screening with a general gynaecological or STI screen, rather than its specific HPV/cervical-abnormality purpose.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Cervical screening catches HPV and pre-cancer before cancer, nothing more.

live_plab_copy.thinking: Chronic anovulation ↓ Little progesterone from ovulation ↓ Unopposed oestrogen on the endometrium ↓ Endometrial overgrowth ↓ Increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, protection against endometrial cancer — the combined pill often used in PMOS is protective, which may confuse, but the condition itself raises endometrial cancer risk.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Anovulation in PMOS means unopposed oestrogen and endometrial hyperplasia risk.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 27-year-old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant develops dysuria and urinary frequency. Urine testing supports a urinary tract infection.

What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Give analgesia and increased fluids, and treat if fever develops
options.B: Prescribe ciprofloxacin as first-line treatment for the UTI
options.C: Defer antibiotics until urine culture confirms the organism
options.D: Treat appropriately because UTI in pregnancy carries additional risks
options.E: Treat if a repeat dipstick in one week remains positive

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Treat appropriately because UTI in pregnancy carries additional risks
live_plab_copy.why_correct: UTI in pregnancy should be treated promptly because untreated infection increases the risk of pyelonephritis and adverse pregnancy outcomes. NICE NG109 advises sending a midstream urine sample for culture before starting an antibiotic suitable for pregnancy (for example nitrofurantoin, avoiding it at term). Source: NICE NG109, Urinary tract infection (lower): antimicrobial prescribing (pregnancy section); NICE CKS, Urinary tract infection (lower) – women, management in pregnancy.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Analgesia relieves symptoms but does not treat the infection, which requires antibiotics in pregnancy. B. Quinolones are avoided in pregnancy; antibiotic choice must take pregnancy into account. C. A culture should be sent, but antibiotics should be started without waiting for the result. E. Delaying treatment risks pyelonephritis and adverse pregnancy outcomes.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Pregnancy frequently changes the threshold for investigation and treatment.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnancy + UTI  ↓  treat appropriately  ↓  consider pregnancy-safe antibiotic choice.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, deferring antibiotics until culture results — a culture should be sent, but in pregnancy treatment starts immediately to prevent pyelonephritis.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Symptomatic UTI in pregnancy: send a culture and start a pregnancy-safe antibiotic straight away.

A pregnant woman who is not known to have had chickenpox is exposed to a child with chickenpox.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Give the MMR vaccine within 72 hours of contact
options.B: Reassure her, as chickenpox is usually mild in adults
options.C: Give the varicella vaccine within 5 days of contact
options.D: Start aciclovir now without checking immunity
options.E: Assess exposure and check varicella antibodies

Varicella can cause serious maternal pneumonitis and fetal varicella syndrome, so reassurance alone is inappropriate. C. Varicella vaccine is live and contraindicated in pregnancy. D. Immunity should be checked first; women with varicella antibodies need no antiviral prophylaxis.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A pregnant woman exposed to chickenpox with uncertain immunity needs urgent varicella IgG testing; if non-immune she needs specialist post-exposure prophylaxis, as maternal varicella can cause severe pneumonitis.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant, no known chickenpox ↓ Contact with a child with chickenpox ↓ Risk of maternal pneumonitis and fetal harm ↓ Confirm significant exposure and immunity ↓ Check varicella antibodies
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, start aciclovir now — prophylaxis may be needed, but many adults are already immune, so check varicella antibodies first; immune women need no treatment.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Chickenpox contact in pregnancy: check varicella IgG before deciding on prophylaxis.

A pregnant woman has persistent vomiting and is unable to keep fluids down. She is clinically dehydrated.

What is the immediate priority?

options.C: Assess and manage dehydration and electrolyte disturbance

live_plab_copy.why_correct: Persistent vomiting in pregnancy with dehydration suggests hyperemesis gravidarum. The priority is to assess and correct fluid and electrolyte disturbance, usually with IV fluids and antiemetics (RCOG Green-top Guideline 69).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Delay risks serious complications. B. Restricting fluids worsens dehydration. D. Persistent vomiting can cause dehydration, electrolyte imbalance and Wernicke's encephalopathy. E. Medicines should be reviewed, not stopped without assessment.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Persistent vomiting in pregnancy with dehydration suggests hyperemesis gravidarum: correct fluids and electrolytes and give antiemetics, with thiamine where indicated to prevent Wernicke's.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant, persistent vomiting ↓ unable to keep fluids down, clinically dehydrated ↓ likely hyperemesis gravidarum with fluid and electrolyte loss ↓ assess and manage dehydration and electrolytes
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, restricting oral fluids — resting the stomach may seem to settle vomiting, but it worsens dehydration; fluids and electrolytes need active correction.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Vomiting in pregnancy with dehydration: rehydrate and correct electrolytes first.

akt_source.stem:
A pregnant woman has persistent vomiting and is unable to keep fluids down. She is clinically dehydrated.

What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Delay assessment until the next antenatal appointment
options.C: Assess and manage dehydration and electrolyte disturbance
options.D: Reassure her that vomiting cannot cause complications
options.E: Stop all pregnancy-related medication without assessment

akt_source.correct_answer: C. Assess and manage dehydration and electrolyte disturbance
akt_source.why_correct: Persistent vomiting in pregnancy with dehydration suggests hyperemesis gravidarum. The priority is to assess and correct fluid and electrolyte disturbance, usually with IV fluids and antiemetics (RCOG Green-top Guideline 69).
akt_source.why_wrong: A. Delay risks serious complications. B. Restricting fluids worsens dehydration. D. Persistent vomiting can cause dehydration, electrolyte imbalance and Wernicke's encephalopathy. E. Medicines should be reviewed, not stopped without assessment.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 29-year-old pregnant woman develops vaginal bleeding and severe abdominal pain. She feels faint and has a rapid pulse. What is the immediate concern?

options.A: Vasovagal syncope

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Hypovolaemic shock from haemorrhage
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Pregnancy-associated bleeding with severe pain, faintness and tachycardia requires urgent assessment and resuscitation for possible significant haemorrhage.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Vasovagal syncope does not explain bleeding and severe abdominal pain. B. Supine hypotension resolves on lateral positioning and does not cause bleeding. C. Threatened miscarriage involves bleeding without haemodynamic compromise. E. Hyperemesis causes vomiting and dehydration, not vaginal bleeding with severe pain.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Bleeding, severe pain, faintness and tachycardia in pregnancy signal haemorrhagic shock, for example from a ruptured ectopic or abruption; resuscitate with ABCDE and call senior help immediately.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnant with vaginal bleeding ↓ Severe abdominal pain ↓ Feels faint with a rapid pulse ↓ Hypovolaemic shock from haemorrhage
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, threatened miscarriage — bleeding in pregnancy suggests it, but threatened miscarriage involves a stable patient, not severe pain with signs of shock.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Pregnancy bleeding plus tachycardia and faintness: treat as haemorrhagic shock.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 63-year-old woman has vaginal bleeding three years after her menopause.

What is the appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Treat as atrophic vaginitis with topical oestrogen first
options.B: Arrange CA125 testing for ovarian cancer as the main step
options.C: Reassure that bleeding is common in the years after menopause
options.D: Investigate the cause, including endometrial pathology
options.E: Repeat assessment if bleeding recurs within six months

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Investigate the cause, including endometrial pathology
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Postmenopausal bleeding (bleeding 12 months or more after the last period) must be investigated, and NICE NG12 (amended 2026) recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for women aged 55 and over with unexplained postmenopausal bleeding that cannot be attributed to HRT. This woman aged 63 needs referral for transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial assessment to exclude endometrial cancer.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Atrophic vaginitis is a common cause, but malignancy must be excluded first. B. Endometrial pathology, not ovarian cancer, is the main concern. C. Bleeding after menopause is not normal and needs investigation. E. A single episode of postmenopausal bleeding needs investigation.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Postmenopausal bleeding needs investigation for endometrial cancer; first-line assessment is transvaginal ultrasound of endometrial thickness, with endometrial sampling when indicated.
live_plab_copy.thinking: > Any postmenopausal bleeding  ↓  investigate.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, atrophic vaginitis treated with topical oestrogen — tempting because atrophy is a common cause, but it can be accepted only after endometrial cancer has been excluded.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Postmenopausal bleeding is never normal: investigate to exclude endometrial cancer.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 34-year-old woman at 33 weeks' gestation presents with severe headache and visual disturbance. Her blood pressure is 170/115 mmHg.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Start oral labetalol and review in the antenatal clinic next week
options.B: Treat as severe hypertension in pregnancy needing urgent care
options.C: Check urine for protein and review in 48 hours if negative
options.D: Give paracetamol for tension headache and recheck BP tomorrow
options.E: Recommend bed rest at home with daily BP checks by the midwife

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Treat as severe hypertension in pregnancy needing urgent care
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Severe hypertension with neurological symptoms in pregnancy is a medical/obstetric emergency and may represent severe pre-eclampsia. Source: NICE NG133, Hypertension in pregnancy.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Severe hypertension with neurological symptoms needs same-day admission, not outpatient review. C. Absence of proteinuria does not exclude pre-eclampsia, and delay is unsafe. D. Severe headache and visual disturbance with a BP of 170/115 mmHg are red flags. E. Home bed rest is insufficient.
live_plab_copy.pearl: NICE identifies severe headache, visual symptoms and other neurological/systemic features as important indicators when considering magnesium sulfate in severe pre-eclampsia.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Pregnancy + severe hypertension + neurological symptoms  ↓  severe pre-eclampsia pathway.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, oral labetalol with clinic review next week — labetalol is a correct drug, but severe hypertension with headache and visual symptoms needs same-day admission.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Severe hypertension with neurological symptoms in pregnancy: urgent admission for possible severe pre-eclampsia.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A postmenopausal woman develops vaginal dryness and discomfort during intercourse.

Which mechanism is most likely?

options.A: Increased progesterone production

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Reduced oestrogen levels
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Oestrogen deficiency after menopause can cause vulvovaginal dryness, irritation and dyspareunia.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Increased progesterone is not the mechanism. B. PTH regulates calcium and phosphate metabolism. C. Aldosterone regulates fluid and electrolyte balance. D. Insulin does not cause menopausal vaginal symptoms.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Genitourinary symptoms of menopause stem from oestrogen deficiency; vaginal oestrogen is effective and can be used alone or alongside systemic HRT.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Postmenopausal ↓ Vaginal dryness and dyspareunia ↓ Vaginal epithelium is oestrogen-dependent ↓ Reduced oestrogen levels
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, increased progesterone production — a sex-hormone change tempts, but progesterone falls after menopause; the driver is oestrogen loss.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Postmenopausal vaginal dryness is due to oestrogen deficiency.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A woman with a positive pregnancy test develops sudden severe abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, tachycardia and hypotension.

What is the priority?

options.A: Arrange an early pregnancy unit appointment for the next morning
options.B: Treat as a ruptured ectopic and arrange emergency management
options.C: Reassure, as pain is common in early pregnancy, and give analgesia
options.D: Repeat the serum hCG in 48 hours to assess viability
options.E: Arrange a routine transvaginal ultrasound later in the week

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Treat as a ruptured ectopic and arrange emergency management
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Positive pregnancy test, acute abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain (from diaphragmatic irritation by haemoperitoneum) and shock suggest a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, which needs immediate resuscitation and emergency gynaecological surgery (NICE NG126).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. A shocked patient cannot wait until the next day; she needs immediate resuscitation and surgery. C. This presentation is not normal early pregnancy pain and indicates a life-threatening emergency. D. Serial hCG is for stable pregnancies of unknown location, not a shocked patient. E. Routine scanning would delay life-saving treatment.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A positive pregnancy test with abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain and shock is a ruptured ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise; resuscitate and arrange emergency surgery without delay.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Positive pregnancy test with sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ Shoulder-tip pain suggests haemoperitoneum irritating the diaphragm ↓ Tachycardia and hypotension mean haemorrhagic shock ↓ Ruptured ectopic: resuscitate and arrange emergency surgery
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, repeating serum hCG in 48 hours — serial hCG is used for stable pregnancies of unknown location, but in a shocked patient it only delays life-saving surgery.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Early pregnancy with pain and shock means ruptured ectopic: resuscitate and arrange emergency surgery.

live_plab_copy.stem: A woman at 31 weeks develops leakage of fluid from the vagina before the onset of labour. What is this called?

options.A: Hyperemesis gravidarum
options.C: Prelabour rupture of membranes at term

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Rupture of membranes before labour and before 37 weeks is preterm prelabour rupture of membranes.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Hyperemesis causes vomiting. C. Term begins at 37 weeks; rupture at 31 weeks is preterm. D. Placental abruption causes bleeding and abdominal pain. E. Placenta praevia causes painless bleeding.
live_plab_copy.pearl: P-PROM is confirmed on speculum examination by pooling of amniotic fluid; avoid digital vaginal examination, and give prophylactic antibiotics such as erythromycin and antenatal corticosteroids.
live_plab_copy.thinking: 31 weeks pregnant ↓ Fluid leaking from the vagina ↓ No labour yet ↓ Before 37 weeks ↓ Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, prelabour rupture of membranes at term — the right event at the wrong gestation; term starts at 37 weeks, so rupture at 31 weeks is preterm.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Rupture before labour and before 37 weeks is preterm prelabour rupture of membranes.
